title: Optimizing Prompts for Large Language Models: A Causal Approach
affiliations: University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, Shanghai Jiaotong University, , University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Optimizing Prompts for Large Language Models: A Causal Approach
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in enterprise workflows, yet their performance remains highly sensitive to prompt design. Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) seeks to mitigate this instability, but existing approaches face two persistent challenges. First, commonly used prompt strategies rely on static instructions that perform well on average but fail to adapt to heterogeneous queries. Second, more dynamic approaches depend on reward models that are fundamentally correlational, confounding prompt effectiveness with query characteristics. As a result, prompts that appear "optimized" in historical data often generalize poorly to novel or complex inputs. We propose Causal Prompt Optimization (CPO), a framework that reframes prompt design as a problem of causal estimation. CPO operates in two stages. First, it learns an offline causal reward model by applying Double Machine Learning (DML) to semantic embeddings of prompts and queries, isolating the causal effect of prompt variations from confounding query attributes, i.e., estimating how model performance would change if the same query were answered under an alternative prompt. Second, it utilizes this unbiased reward signal to guide a resource-efficient search for query-specific prompts without relying on costly online evaluation. We evaluate CPO across benchmarks in mathematical reasoning, visualization, and data analytics. CPO consistently outperforms human-engineered prompts and state-of-the-art automated optimizers. The gains are driven primarily by improved robustness on hard queries, where existing methods tend to deteriorate. Beyond performance, CPO fundamentally reshapes the economics of prompt optimization: by shifting evaluation from real-time model execution to an offline causal model, it enables high-precision, per-query customization at a fraction of the inference cost required by online methods. Together, these results establish causal inference as a scalable foundation for reliable and cost-efficient prompt optimization in enterprise LLM deployments under heterogeneous and shifting query distributions.

title: The New Marketing Reality: Deconstructing Success Factors in Metaverse Customer Engagement
affiliations: University of Petra, University of Petra and Petra University

detail.title: The New Marketing Reality: Deconstructing Success Factors in Metaverse Customer Engagement
detail.abstract: The meteoric rise of the metaverse as an immersive digital realm has created unprecedented opportunities for innovative marketing strategies and enhanced customer engagement. This study empirically investigates the dynamic relationships between three key metaverse marketing strategies—virtual brand experiences (VBE), AI personalization (AP), and virtual influencers (VI)—and customer engagement, focusing on the critical mediating role of digital readiness. Using a comprehensive survey of metaverse users (N=490), we employ rigorous statistical analyses to test a theoretically grounded framework based on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) model. Our findings reveal that all three marketing strategies significantly influence customer engagement, with digital readiness serving as a partial mediator in these relationships. Virtual influencers demonstrate the strongest direct effect on customer engagement (β =0.246), while virtual brand experiences show the highest proportion of mediation through digital readiness (17.7%). These results enrich our understanding of the psychological mechanisms through which metaverse marketing impacts customer engagement, extending the S-O-R framework into virtual environments. This study contributes to the nascent literature on metaverse marketing by identifying effective strategies for fostering customer engagement and highlighting the importance of digital readiness in maximizing marketing effectiveness. For practitioners, our research provides evidence-based insights for developing targeted metaverse marketing strategies that consider customers’ varying levels of digital readiness. By strategically enhancing both customer experiences and digital capabilities, marketers can optimize engagement in the rapidly evolving metaverse landscape.

title: Enhancing Consumer Trust in AI-Generated Marketing Content for Scientific Innovations,An Interdisciplinary Framework Integrating Marketing, Data Science, and Behavioral Psychology

detail.title: Enhancing Consumer Trust in AI-Generated Marketing Content for Scientific Innovations,An Interdisciplinary Framework Integrating Marketing, Data Science, and Behavioral Psychology
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing marketing strategies dramatically; however, its usage to advertise scientific innovations such as biotechnological solutions and climate, resilient technologies leads to significant concerns regarding consumer trust loss. This research explores the interaction of three disciplines marketing, data science, and behavioral psychologyto create a framework for the ethical use of AI, generated content in communication of science.Based on a mixed, methods approach, which involved surveys of 1, 200 consumers from tech, savvy demographics and AI simulation experiments, we pinpointed the main trust barriers: perceived inauthenticity (42% of respondents) and misinformation risks (35%). The "Trust, Infused AI Canvas" model we suggest merges the algorithmic transparency element from data science with the narrative empathy component from psychology, thus demonstrating a 28% increase of trust metrics during pilot campaigns of a biotech firm.The results show that content created through a hybrid human, AI approach is more effective in achieving higher levels of perceived genuineness than fully automated outputs, thereby providing practical insights for marketers on how to handle the trust deficit challenge in science, driven commerce. This investigation fills an important gap and calls for regulatory frameworks that prioritize collaboration across disciplines as a way to ensure sustainable consumer engagement in an AI, augmented marketplace.

title: Brand Narrative Structure Migration and Capital Market Reactions: Evidence from DR Group
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and Hunan University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Brand Narrative Structure Migration and Capital Market Reactions: Evidence from DR Group
detail.abstract: In contemporary marketing practice, the formation and fluctuation of brand value increasingly depend on users’understanding of brand content. Such fluctuation not only reflects short-term shifts in user sentiment, but may also arise from structural changes in the semantic frameworks through which users interpret brand narratives. This paper proposes the concept of Brand Cognition Drift (BCD) to depict the structural migration in users semantic understanding of brand narratives.Using monthly data from user reviews between 2022 and 2024, we first employ an LDA model and conduct perplexity and coherence checks, then apply the dynamic topic model BERTopic to extract high-dimensional semantic topics from user comments about the brand on Weibo. On this basis, we build a composite LDA–BERTopic text analysis framework, and construct a monthly Cognition Drift Index (CDI). Taking DR Group (301177.SZ) as a case, we examine the relationship between CDI and the firm’s performance in the capital market.Empirical results show that CDI is stably and negatively associated with price-to-book ratio, stock price, and market capitalization, and carries certain lagged information content. This paper quantifies the structural risk of corporate brand narratives into testable indicators, provides reproducible evidence from the context of Chinese social media, and offers a text-based monitoring pathway for brand risk early warning and market value management.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a minimal, practical approach to stabilizing decision-making processes under conditions of high uncertainty. Instead of modeling cognition, optimizing behavior, or increasing system complexity, the approach introduces simple protocol-based constraints that reduce destructive decision modes such as delay, oscillation, and impulsive action. The proposed protocols do not determine what decision should be made. They specify the conditions under which a decision is allowed to occur. The framework is exploratory and intended for discussion and experimental use in human or hybrid decision systems.

detail.abstract: Exit planning for closely held enterprises has traditionally emphasized valuation, tax efficiency, and transactional execution. However, increased retrospective scrutiny arising from Small Business Administration (SBA) programs and related federal oversight has exposed structural weaknesses in conventional exit strategies. Many legally valid transactions fail under audit conditions due to insufficient documentation of economic substance, ambiguous control transitions, and governance designs that prioritize form over demonstrable economic progression. This paper introduces an Economic Substance Framework for Audit-Safe Exit Pathways, a governance-based model designed to align exit planning with regulatory expectations and retrospective audit interpretation. Grounded in agency theory, stewardship theory, and transaction cost economics, the framework organizes exit activity into layered components that preserve economic substance, clarify control termination, and enhance forensic readiness. The framework has been field-tested through implementation in operating agreement documentation for a South Carolina-domiciled enterprise, demonstrating practical feasibility. Further illustrations examine application to service-sector exits and trust-integrated succession structures.

title: LUCIDITY Beat Map: Spatial-Temporal Visualization of AI Output Degradation Patterns

detail.title: LUCIDITY Beat Map: Spatial-Temporal Visualization of AI Output Degradation Patterns
detail.abstract: As generative AI systems produce increasing volumes of text, the challenge of systematic quality assessment has become critical. Existing AI output evaluation tools provide aggregate quality scores but fail to localize degradation patterns within content structure. We present LUCIDITY Beat Map, a novel spatial-temporal visualization system that segments AI-generated content into discrete timeline units and displays degradation intensity across six distinct quality dimensions. Powered by ACTS (Automated Convergence Triangulation System), a 14-vector analysis engine, Beat Map transforms abstract quality metrics into actionable visual intelligence, enabling users to identify precisely WHERE quality degrades rather than merely HOW MUCH. Through analysis of diverse AI outputs across multiple generation models, we demonstrate that degradation patterns cluster non-randomly within document structure, with distinct signatures for repetition, vagueness, intent decay, confidence inflation, voice degradation, and entropy collapse. Beat Map achieves deterministic, reproducible analysis across 50+ file formats without requiring model retraining or architectural modification. This work establishes a new paradigm for AI output quality control: spatial quality mapping as a complement to scalar scoring, with implications for content governance, automated editing, and AI system evaluation.

title: Managing Road Safety in Gig Work: Can Recommender Systems Save Lives?
affiliations: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, National University of Singapore (NUS), Woowa Bros and Woowa Bros

detail.title: Managing Road Safety in Gig Work: Can Recommender Systems Save Lives?
detail.abstract:
Problem Definition: Food-delivery drivers make frequent, complex decisions about which tasks to accept, often while on the move. This cognitive load can lead to distraction and increase the risk of accidents. Recommender systems, which streamline task selection by offering optimized suggestions, may help mitigate this risk.
We investigate whether adopting a task recommender system reduces accident rates among food-delivery drivers. 
We also examine what happens after adoption--specifically, whether drivers maintain adherence to recommendations after experiencing road accidents. Traumatic events such as accidents can prompt individuals to reclaim a sense of personal agency. Because recommender systems may be perceived as undermining that agency, we explore whether accidents lead to reduced system adherence. 
Methodology / Results: We partnered with South Korea’s largest food-delivery platform and analyzed behavioral and safety data from 8,883 drivers, some of whom adopted a task recommender system. Using a quasi-experimental design and a Difference-in-Differences framework combined with Propensity Score Matching, we compared outcomes between adopters (treatment) and matched non-adopters (control).
Drivers who adopted the system experienced an 85% reduction in at-fault accidents and a 65% reduction in total accidents. They also saw a 9.52% increase in earnings and a 0.84 percentage point increase in on-time deliveries. However, within the adopters, adherence to recommendations declined by 2.9% following an accident.
Our study provides the first empirical evidence on how adopting a task recommender system impacts the physical safety of gig workers, and how road accidents impact the post-adoption recommendation adherence. 
Managerial Implications: Platforms can leverage these findings to educate and nudge gig workers toward adopting recommender systems.
More critically, the observed post-accident decline in adherence creates a negative feedback loop: accidents reduce adherence, increasing cognitive load and the risk of future accidents. Platforms must design interventions that restore a sense of agency after accidents and improve adherence.

detail.abstract:
Jurisprudential Lineage and the Need for Systemic Accountability: 

From the earliest foundations of constitutional democracy, legal doctrine has sought to ensure that governmental power is exercised fairly, rationally, and accountably. Traditional jurisprudential tools—such as due process balancing tests, reasonableness standards, evidentiary rules, and deference doctrines—address discrete components of fairness within adjudication and administration. Yet these doctrines were not designed to evaluate systemic failures in decision-making integrity, particularly where institutional bias, procedural fragmentation, or incomplete records obscure accountability.

This Article introduces the Anwar Balance Test (ABT), a comprehensive legal framework for assessing whether a decision-making process is structurally fair and accountable from initiation to resolution. Building upon established principles of procedural justice, ABT shifts the analytical focus from isolated legal defects to the integrity of the system as a whole. Unlike existing tests—such as Mathews v. Eldridge balancing, Chevron deference, Daubert evidentiary standards, or use-of-force reasonableness inquiries—ABT evaluates whether institutional design, information flow, and procedural safeguards collectively preserve justice rather than merely approximate it.

By providing a structured method to measure systemic accountability, ABT offers courts, regulators, and policymakers a doctrinal tool capable of addressing modern governance failures that traditional jurisprudence leaves unresolved. The framework is intended to enhance judicial clarity, reduce institutional bias, and restore public confidence in legal decision-making where procedural legitimacy itself is in question.

detail.abstract: The present study delineates the analysis and design of an innovative Vision-to-Text Automator, a hybrid Optical Character Recognition (OCR) system developed to facilitate intelligent document retrieval through the application of Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagrams. In response to the burgeoning dependence on digital document processing, this research addresses prevalent limitations observed in traditional OCR technologies, including suboptimal accuracy with complex document layouts and a lack of integrated conversational interfaces. The findings underscore the efficacy of UML in enhancing system functionality, user interaction, and information extraction, ultimately contributing to the advancement of responsive and user-centric document digitization platforms.

The Global Memory Standard (GMS) establishes a permanent, quantum-authenticated archival doctrine designed to replace migration-dependent semiconductor storage with a millennia-scale crystalline substrate. It addresses a foundational vulnerability in modern governance and infrastructure: constitutional records, scientific baselines, financial systems, and artificial-intelligence artifacts of enduring significance are currently entrusted to storage media engineered for short lifespans, continuous power draw, and frequent rewrite cycles. As computation—particularly AI-scale inference and model persistence—accelerates beyond the practical limits of Moore-era architectures, this inheritance now generates systemic risk across national energy grids, institutional continuity, and international stability.

This pressure is illustrated through conservative stress-testing. Under AI-scale demand trajectories of approximately 2.5–3.0% annual growth, electricity demand outpaces generation expansion within a single planning horizon, compressing the timeframe in which conventional capacity additions alone can preserve grid adequacy. Reframing this challenge, GMS demonstrates that disciplined architectural choices can convert electricity expenditure into national capability: avoided continuous-power storage loads function not merely as efficiency gains, but as reclaimed economic and strategic capacity per unit of energy consumed. Extending the analysis globally, GMS presents an ordinal, non-competitive assessment of when selected nations are likely to encounter structural infrastructure stress as AI adoption scales faster than supporting energy, data, and governance systems. Together, these findings establish the strategic importance of non-capacity-intensive solutions—architectural optimization and force-multiplying infrastructure—within long-horizon energy and AI planning.

Drawing on National Academies guidance on federal data preservation, UNESCO’s Memory of the World principles, NIST outcome-based governance frameworks, and standards-driven international coordination models, GMS defines a legally and diplomatically interoperable architecture for global permanence. At its core is the Quantum-Embedded Memory Crystal (QEMC): a passive, near-zero-energy storage substrate capable of quantum-secured verification, resistance to thermal and radiative degradation, and integrity retention across technological cycles. By decoupling archival memory from continuous power consumption, GMS reduces baseload grid demand, mitigates AI-driven energy shocks, and introduces a stability multiplier consistent with the principle that infrastructural symmetry reinforces geopolitical equilibrium.

At the governance frontier, GMS functions as an infrastructural precursor to emerging artificial-intelligence oversight frameworks. It preserves continuity of record without asserting autonomy, intent, or agency, ensuring that future artificial systems do not compete with human societies for finite energy resources or interpretive authority. Legally, GMS offers a standard-portable framework compatible with U.S. federal administrative requirements, NATO resilience doctrine, and United Nations treaty structures governing global public goods. Diplomatically, its Any Nation Protocol ensures that no state, alliance, or corporation can exert hegemonic control over civilizational memory.

The Global Memory Standard concludes that a quantum-authenticated crystalline memory substrate is not merely a technological advancement, but a form of civilizational infrastructure—one that stabilizes energy systems, preserves documentary heritage, reinforces sovereign equality, and ensures that both human and emerging non-biological intelligences inherit a durable, neutral, and law-governed memory architecture for the century ahead.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is no longer merely an analytical tool-it is an active variable reshaping the cognitive architecture, emotional weightage, and risk calculus underlying executive decision-making. This paper posits that AI introduces a second operating system in leadership cognition, one that rewires the heuristics through which leaders interpret uncertainty, project outcomes, and assign value to strategic choices. Integrating behavioral economics with computational decision theory, we construct a model of Decision DNA to demonstrate how automated intelligence modifies judgment pathways across three axes: (1) risk perception and tolerance, (2) bias attenuation or amplification, and (3) emotional-cognitive load redistribution in high-stakes environments. We argue that AI's predictive precision alters not only what leaders decide but how they arrive at decisions-shifting leadership behaviour from intuition-anchored reasoning toward algorithmic logic, hybrid cognition, and probabilistic foresight. Drawing upon empirical insights, neuro-behavioral mechanisms, and case-based observation from digital-first enterprises, the study highlights both the competence gains and capability erosion that emerge when leaders co-process decisions with intelligent systems. Key implications include the emergence of Synthetic Judgment as a new leadership competency and the imperative of emotional governance to mitigate over-reliance on machine-driven rationality. The paper concludes that the next frontier of organizational advantage will not be technological deployment alone, but the deliberate design of a leadership ecosystem where human intuition, AI-assisted reasoning, and behavioral discipline co-evolve. When understood as a behavioral algorithm rather than a technological artifact, AI becomes a force that reshapes the executive mind-reconfiguring judgment, risk appetite, accountability, and ultimately, the future of leadership itself.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become deeply embedded in organizational decision-making, leadership is undergoing a quiet but consequential shift. What were once tools designed to support human judgment are increasingly positioned to substitute it. Existing research on AI in leadership has largely focused on ethical risks, algorithmic bias, and transparency concerns. However, these approaches fail to adequately explain a more insidious phenomenon: the gradual displacement of human authority in strategic and high-stakes decisions without formal delegation, awareness, or accountability. This paper introduces Decision Substitution as a novel behavioural leadership risk, defined as the progressive replacement of human judgment by AI-generated outputs in contexts where leaders remain formally accountable but are no longer the true decision-makers. Drawing on behavioural decision theory, leadership studies, and human-AI interaction research, the paper argues that decision substitution emerges not from technological malfunction, but from predictable behavioural mechanisms-authority bias, cognitive offloading, moral outsourcing, performance pressure, and diffusion of responsibility-amplified by intelligent systems.

detail.abstract: Online tax compliance systems have emerged as critical tools for enhancing tax collection efficiency and compliance, particularly in developing and emerging economies where traditional tax administration faces structural and operational challenges. These digital platforms facilitate streamlined reporting, reduce opportunities for tax evasion, and improve transparency in revenue generation, thereby supporting broader economic development goals. This study employs a case study analysis and comparative approach to evaluate the effectiveness of online tax compliance systems across selected developing economies. Evaluation metrics focus on system adoption rates, user satisfaction, compliance levels, and operational efficiency. The findings indicate that while online tax systems significantly improve compliance and administrative efficiency, their effectiveness is often constrained by challenges such as limited user adoption, low trust in digital platforms, inadequate technical infrastructure, and gaps in taxpayer education. The study underscores the importance of addressing these barriers to maximize the benefits of digital tax systems. The insights gained have practical implications for policymakers aiming to enhance revenue collection, for developers seeking to design user-friendly and secure digital tax platforms, and for researchers pursuing further exploration into digital governance and taxation. By identifying both successes and challenges, this research contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how online tax compliance systems can be leveraged to strengthen fiscal administration in resource-constrained contexts.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Tax Fraud

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Tax Fraud
detail.abstract: This study investigates the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in detecting tax fraud, a critical challenge for modern revenue authorities. By employing a comprehensive literature review, comparative analysis of AI techniques, and examination of relevant case studies, the research evaluates the effectiveness of AI-driven tools in enhancing tax compliance. Findings indicate that AI significantly improves fraud detection accuracy, minimizes compliance gaps, and identifies complex, previously undetectable fraud networks. Techniques such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and network analysis demonstrate superior performance compared to traditional audit methods, enabling authorities to proactively detect suspicious activities and optimize resource allocation. The study also highlights challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy concerns, algorithm transparency, and the need for skilled personnel to interpret AI outputs. Despite these challenges, the integration of AI into tax administration emerges as a transformative approach, offering substantial efficiency gains and reinforcing the integrity of tax systems. The results underscore the necessity for policymakers and tax authorities to adopt AI-driven frameworks while ensuring robust governance and ethical standards. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on digital taxation and offers practical insights for enhancing fraud detection mechanisms in increasingly complex fiscal environments (Ariyibi et al., 2024).

title: Cryptocurrency Taxation Frameworks and Compliance Issues

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Taxation Frameworks and Compliance Issues
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of cryptocurrencies has introduced unprecedented challenges for global taxation systems, necessitating a reevaluation of existing frameworks (Yan, 2024). This study investigates the effectiveness of current taxation policies on digital assets, focusing on compliance difficulties and regulatory gaps that hinder equitable revenue collection (Olabanji, 2023). Through a comparative analysis of multiple jurisdictions, the research identifies significant inconsistencies in cryptocurrency taxation approaches, ranging from complete regulatory absence to fragmented or overlapping frameworks. Findings indicate that decentralized platforms and peer-to-peer transactions often exhibit limited compliance, exacerbating the risk of tax evasion and revenue loss. Additionally, the study highlights the critical role of digital tools and taxpayer education in enhancing compliance, as technological sophistication and limited awareness impede effective reporting and enforcement (Adelakun et al., 2024; Ness, 2024). Based on these insights, the paper recommends the adoption of harmonised international regulations, the integration of blockchain-based monitoring systems for transparent transaction tracking, and targeted taxpayer education initiatives to improve understanding and adherence to tax obligations (Abbas et al., 2024). By addressing both structural and behavioral challenges, these measures aim to strengthen the capacity of tax authorities to manage digital asset taxation effectively. The research underscores the urgency of coordinated policy action and technological innovation to ensure that taxation frameworks remain relevant and enforceable in the rapidly evolving digital economy.

detail.abstract: This study provides a critical, evidence-based examination of how cross-border digital trade affects national tax revenue systems, with particular emphasis on compliance challenges, enforcement constraints, and existing policy gaps. Drawing on a systematic review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the analysis evaluates how digital business models, cross-border data flows, and platform-based value creation interact with conventional tax frameworks. The study synthesises evidence from global and developing-economy contexts to assess the implications for corporate income tax and consumption-based taxes. The findings reveal that although digital trade significantly expands economic activity and international market participation, it simultaneously undermines traditional tax bases. This erosion is largely driven by profit shifting facilitated by the mobility of intangible assets, the difficulty of taxing value generated through data, and regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions (Hanappi et al., 2024). Empirical evidence highlights persistent compliance and enforcement challenges, particularly in countries with limited administrative capacity (Adebiyi, 2023), while the absence of physical presence requirements allows many digital firms to escape effective taxation (Sun & Trefler, 2023). Insights from the Digital Economy and Tax Justice study further demonstrate widening disparities in tax revenue mobilisation. The study concludes that effective taxation in the digital era requires coordinated international tax frameworks, enhanced digital monitoring tools, and adaptive tax policies that move beyond conventional physical-presence rules.

detail.abstract: Despite explosive parameter growth and extended context windows, current large language models (LLMs) remain trapped by the dual defects of "goldfish memory" and "intent contamination." Building upon the original Temporal Dimension Expansion, this extended edition systematically diagnoses the fatal consequences of intent contamination-from theme-mixing in user interactions to potential doomsday scenarios in physical robots (such as the "baby-in-oven" tragedy caused by multi-task switching failures). The author proposes a comprehensive three-layer framework: a temporal memory layer (decay, compression, hooks, hierarchy), an intent routing layer (detection, isolation, multi-threading, task persistence), and a user relationship layer (profile, warmth, continuous consciousness). The conclusion pronounces a harsh verdict: without intent isolation and continuous consciousness, LLMs will never achieve godhood; premature deployment in the physical world will inevitably breed catastrophe. This is not merely technical optimization-it is the life-or-death baseline for AGI safety.

Findings reveal that specific intersections and transit corridors are disproportionately susceptible to disruptions, highlighting areas where targeted interventions can significantly improve network robustness. Simulation results further demonstrate how cascading failures can propagate through the network, underscoring the importance of preemptive planning. The results reveal significant hotspots of environmental risk, particularly in low-lying and densely populated zones, with strong correlations between risk exposure and socio-demographic factors such as income levels and population density. Critical areas for intervention were highlighted, providing actionable insights for targeted mitigation strategies. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of GIS-based approaches in visualising and prioritising environmental vulnerabilities, offering valuable guidance for policymakers, urban planners, and disaster management agencies to enhance resilience in informal settlements.

Using a combination of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) analysis, remote sensing imagery, field surveys, and a review of zoning regulations, the study identifies spatial and temporal trends in land-use transformation and areas of regulatory non-compliance. The findings reveal significant shifts from agricultural and undeveloped lands to residential, commercial, and industrial uses, with notable concentrations of non-compliance in peripheral and high-demand urban zones. Socioeconomic factors, such as population growth, housing demand, and informal development, alongside environmental drivers, including topography and proximity to infrastructure, were found to influence these patterns (Biłozor et al., 2024). The study concludes that urban growth frequently outpaces existing regulatory mechanisms, highlighting the need for proactive monitoring, targeted enforcement, and adaptive urban planning strategies. Effective integration of spatial analysis with regulatory oversight is essential to guide sustainable urban development and mitigate the adverse effects of unplanned expansion.

Urban flood susceptibility assessment has therefore become a critical tool for supporting sustainable land-use planning and disaster risk reduction strategies (Cai et al., 2024). This study applied a GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process and weighted overlay techniques to model urban flood susceptibility (Nguyen et al., 2024). Multiple spatial data layers, including topography, land use and land cover, drainage density, rainfall intensity, and proximity to water bodies, were standardized and integrated within a GIS environment (Wu et al., 2024). Criterion weights were derived using pairwise comparisons to reflect the relative influence of physical and anthropogenic factors on flood occurrence (Cai et al., 2024). The resulting flood susceptibility map revealed distinct spatial patterns, with high-risk zones concentrated in low-lying areas characterized by dense drainage networks and extensive impervious surfaces (Nguyen et al., 2024). Land-use change and inadequate drainage infrastructure emerged as dominant contributors to elevated flood susceptibility (Wu et al., 2024). Overall, the findings demonstrate that GIS-based MCDA provides a transparent, systematic, and decision-oriented framework for urban flood risk assessment and planning (Cai et al., 2024).

title: Graph Thinking: Network Cognition and Strategic Leadership in AI-Enabled Organizations

detail.title: Graph Thinking: Network Cognition and Strategic Leadership in AI-Enabled Organizations
detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations function as complex networks, yet leadership cognition remains dominated by linear metaphors that assume sequential causality and hierarchical control. This article introduces Graph Thinking as a multi-dimensional leadership capability comprising cognitive, analytical, and behavioral components that enable leaders to perceive, analyze, and deliberately shape organizational network structures. We position Graph Thinking at the intersection of systems thinking, social network analysis, and ecosystem strategy, arguing that it synthesizes these traditions while extending them to address the specific challenges of artificial intelligence deployment. Drawing on network science and strategic management theory, we develop a multi-level framework specifying how Graph Thinking manifests at individual, organizational, and ecosystem levels, with explicit attention to network dynamics and temporal evolution. Through illustrative thought experiments spanning diverse organizational contexts, we demonstrate how network properties function as diagnostic instruments for strategic decision-making. We argue that AI integration creates conditions that may reward explicit network mapping, while acknowledging this relationship is contingent and politically contested. The article contributes to strategic management literature by specifying measurement approaches for future empirical research, addressing power dynamics inherent in network legibility efforts, and providing actionable developmental frameworks. We conclude with boundary conditions, limitations, and directions for empirical validation.

detail.abstract: Classical strategy theory implicitly assumes rational competition, where firms exit markets when returns fall below opportunity cost. This paper argues that under non-rational competition, execution, scale, and efficiencyno longer determine long-term success. Instead, competitive firewalls—structural mechanisms that neutralize competition rather than outperform it—become decisive. We redefine competitive advantage as the ability to preserve cash-flowlongevityunder sustained competitive pressure. We further argue that cash itself functions as strategic optionality, enabling firms toavoid forced participation in destructive competition. Finally, we demonstrate whycompetitive firewalls cannot function without appropriate institutional protection, and why government policy plays a critical role in preventing involution.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the paradoxical state of U.S. tech policy under the second Trump administration, where despite campaign promises and initial executive actions aimed at deregulation, many appointees continue to pursue aggressive regulatory approaches reminiscent of the Biden administration. The paper highlights how the American technology sector represents a remarkable economic success story that has thrived under historically light-touch regulation, contributing significantly to national prosperity through job creation, innovation, and global competitiveness. detail.abstract: The global shift towards climate-conscious development has fundamentally reshaped the conceptual and regulatory boundaries of the Blue Economy, placing offshore oil and gas activities under increasing legal, environmental, and policy scrutiny. In Nigeria, where offshore hydrocarbons remain central to national revenue generation and energy security, the core challenge lies in reconciling continued offshore petroleum operations with climate constraints, environmental protection imperatives, and sustainable ocean governance. This study critically examines the positioning of offshore oil and gas within Nigeria's climate-constrained Blue Economy, assessing the adequacy of existing legal and institutional frameworks in facilitating an effective and just energy transition. Adopting a doctrinal and analytical methodology, the research interrogates Nigeria's offshore petroleum governance architecture, with particular emphasis on climate responsiveness, environmental accountability, and transition-oriented regulatory design. The analysis focuses on offshore emissions governance, environmental risk allocation, decommissioning and asset repurposing of offshore infrastructure, liability for marine pollution, and the integration of alternative offshore energy pathways within Blue Economy governance structures. Drawing insight from Nigeria's offshore regulatory regime and evolving international climate and ocean governance norms, this study evaluates the implications of maintaining hydrocarbon-centred legal frameworks in a climate-constrained ocean economy. The findings reveal that while Nigeria's offshore oil and gas framework continues to prioritise extractive efficiency and revenue optimisation, it remains fragmented and insufficiently aligned with climate transition objectives, resulting in weak climate accountability, limited financial liability for environmental damage, and constrained pathways for low-carbon offshore energy integration. The study recommends, among others, the establishment of enforceable climate and environmental liability regimes, strengthened inter-agency coordination and robust Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) systems, and the integration of transitional fuels and offshore renewable energy within offshore petroleum governance, thereby positioning offshore hydrocarbons as transitional rather than dominant components of Nigeria's ocean-based development strategy.

detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs and critically evaluates John Stuart Mill's arguments for freedom of expression and against paternalistic coercion as articulated in On Liberty. Mill contends that silencing dissenting opinions is unjust regardless of their truth, and that coercive interference with individual conduct is permissible only to prevent harm to others. By grounding liberty in human fallibility, the epistemic value of dissent, and respect for individual agency, Mill offers a principled account of the limits of social and political authority. The paper argues that while Mill's arguments successfully establish liberty as a strong presumptive constraint on coercion, they rely on assumptions about rational capacity and social conditions that limit their applicability in contexts marked by structural inequality and indirect harm. Mill's framework is thus defended as foundational but incomplete, requiring supplementation rather than rejection.

title: Deference Due? "Considers" and the Insurrection Act

detail.title: Deference Due? "Considers" and the Insurrection Act

publicationDetails.detailsText: Univ. of Wisconsin Legal Studies Research Paper No. 1903
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Wisconsin Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This article argues that courts do not owe substantial deference when the President seeks to deploy the military domestically under three of the Insurrection Act’s four trigger provisions. The exception is Section 252, which authorizes deployment “[w]henever the President considers” that has become “impracticable to enforce the laws . . . by the ordinary course of judicial proceedings.” This Article defends that claim through analysis of the Act’s text, statutory history, and legislative history.

The core argument turns on a single word of the Insurrection Act: “considers.” When, and only when, a trigger is keyed to what the President “considers,” courts owe deference. Two negative-implication arguments clarify and strengthen that inference. First, Congress used “considers” in Section 252’s judicial-proceedings trigger, but withheld comparable language from every other trigger, signaling that Section 252 is the sole grant of trigger deference. The statutory and legislative history confirm that this was no accident: Section 252’s “considers” traces to an 1861 amendment that added discretionary language to the judicial-proceedings trigger.  This language was widely understood as necessary to resolve controversy over whether the President could deploy force against the seceding States at the civil war’s outset.

Second, where Congress uses “considers” elsewhere in the Act, it does so to confer deference over the choice and scale of forces (“means deference”), not over whether the trigger is satisfied.  Using ‘considers’ for means while omitting it from triggers underscores that Sections 251 and 253 withhold trigger deference by design. The withholding of trigger deference from Section 253 in particular has a structural logic: Section 253 is the only trigger provision that lacks any comparable ex ante check by another institution, making judicial scrutiny especially necessary ex post.  And because Section 253(2) is the Act’s broadest and most abuse-prone trigger, that judicial check is especially crucial.

title:
Growth Quality, Extrapolability, and the Valuation Trap of Involution

Why Firms Can Grow While Their Valuation Stagnates
affiliations: Fan Ge Institute

detail.title:
Growth Quality, Extrapolability, and the Valuation Trap of Involution

Why Firms Can Grow While Their Valuation Stagnates
detail.abstract:
Persistent margin erosion and valuation stagnation frequently occur even as firms continue to grow in revenue and scale. Conventional explanations attribute this phenomenon to market mispricing, insufficient execution, or temporary competitive pressure. This paper argues instead that such outcomes reflect a structural problem: the deterioration of growth quality. 

We develop a structural interpretation of valuation metrics, arguing that price-to-earnings (P/E) and price-to-book (P/B) ratios function not as valuation formulas, but as market judgments about extrapolability—the plausibility that current earnings can be extended into the future without amplifying systemic risk or organizational fragility. We distinguish growth quantity from growth quality, and propose that low-quality growth is characterized by the erosion of replicability and strategic optionality, even as short-term performance improves. 

A critical concept introduced in this paper is “decline during growth”—a phase in which revenue and cash flow remain positive while growth acceleration weakens and structural constraints begin to surface. We argue that valuation compression during this phase is not a market failure, but a rational response to declining extrapolability.

 By reframing valuation as a structural judgment rather than a mechanical calculation, this paper provides a foundation for understanding involution as a predictable outcome of growth that undermines its own future. The analysis sets the stage for subsequent papers on governance transition and competitive dynamics under non-rational competition.

detail.abstract: We conceptualize equity incentive contracting as a dynamic process in which contracting frictions limit the speed at which equity incentives adjust to target levels. Slower adjustment speeds imply more prolonged deviations from value-maximizing targets and thus more severe negative effects on future performance. We find that contracting frictions significantly slow the speed of adjustment to target incentives (SOA). Consistent with frictions prolonging the persistence of deviations from target, we find that contracting frictions magnify the negative influence of deviations on future firm performance. Further, we find that the influence of contracting frictions on SOA operates through boards’ equity grant decisions. Our dynamic contracting perspective offers new insight into the relation between CEO incentives and firm performance by providing novel evidence that the speed of convergence to target incentives is a defining feature of the dynamic contracting process that translates inefficiency effects of contracting frictions into lower future performance.

title: Business Leaders’ Perception of Digital Transformation in Emerging Economies: On Leader and Technology Interplay

detail.title: Business Leaders’ Perception of Digital Transformation in Emerging Economies: On Leader and Technology Interplay
detail.abstract: The general public dissimilarly interprets the same phenomena in diverse cultures, and leaders’ standpoints also differ about these phenomena. Because of unequal advancement and cultural diversity, a specific welfare level or geography perceives digital transformation radically disparate from others. In advanced economies, leaders typically tend to begin to understand the vitality of digital assets. But the understanding may show differences in an emerging economy. Naturally, the factors such as the type of industry and globalization level of the companies can cause these differences. But a survey in a widespread sector can still help to project business leaders’ and managers’ perceptions of digital transformation in emerging economies, thus pinpointing some of their differences with advanced economies. Two questions come fore at this point: Do business leaders focus on or are aware of the products and ideas of current technologies, and do they appropriately construe these ideas and products? Interviewing leaders in an emerging economy like Turkey has revealed that they predominantly tend to identify digital transformation with social media. Although digital transformation is related to social media, it is not limited to it. There are state-of-the-art technologies. But in such geographies, leaders require time to possess digital and technological consciousness. On the other hand, in this new world order, leadership has reached a point that there is a need for ultimate leaders. The ones that originate from the very elements of this disruptive environment and the ones that rise with distinguishing skills and epoch-making perspectives. Furthermore, learning and performance are indispensable parameters for leaders in times of digital transformation. This article underlines the significant factors that impact these parameters.

detail.abstract: Board independence is widely cited as a cornerstone of good governance in the not-for-profit (NFP) and community services sector. Yet, in practice, independence is often reduced to a narrow compliance test focused on formal conflicts of interest, tenure, or organisational distance, rather than understood as a deeper governance capability that enables purpose, equity, and impact. This paper argues that prevailing approaches to board independence are insufficient for the complexity, moral authority, and accountability demanded of contemporary NFP organisations. Drawing on Australian and international governance practice, the paper reframes board independence as a multidimensional construct, - structural, relational, cultural, and cognitive - essential to purposeful governance. It further explores how evidence-informed decision-making and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools can strengthen, rather than erode, independent judgment when appropriately governed. The paper concludes that truly independent boards are not those most removed from mission, but those best equipped to steward it with integrity, courage, and foresight.

Like all the other organisms, they communicate with the outside world. On one side, leaders affect the outside world, and on the other, leaders are also affected by it. title: The Influence of Perceived Organizational Support, Employee Well-Being, and Career Development on Turnover Intention Among Zillennial Employees: The Mediating Role of Employee Engagement

detail.title: The Influence of Perceived Organizational Support, Employee Well-Being, and Career Development on Turnover Intention Among Zillennial Employees: The Mediating Role of Employee Engagement
detail.abstract: The retention of Zillennial employees (born 1990-2005) presents significant challenges for contemporary organizations navigating competitive labor markets. This study investigates the relationships among perceived organizational support (POS), employee well-being (EWB), career development (CD), employee engagement (EE), and turnover intention (TI) within this workforce segment in Indonesia. Grounded in social exchange theory and complemented by conservation of resources theory, this research employed a quantitative cross-sectional survey design, collecting data from 360 Zillennial employees across multiple industries. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) tested the hypothesized relationships. Results indicate that POS (β =-0.285, p < 0.001) and CD (β =-0.198, p < 0.01) demonstrate significant negative direct effects on turnover intention, while EWB shows no significant direct relationship (β =-0.082, p > 0.05). All three antecedent variables significantly predicted employee engagement, which exhibited a strong negative relationship with turnover intention (β =-0.387, p < 0.001). Mediation analyses confirmed that employee engagement fully mediates the well-being-turnover relationship and partially mediates the effects of POS and CD. The model explained 64.8% of variance in turnover intention. These findings suggest that organizations seeking to retain Zillennial talent in Indonesia should prioritize organizational support systems, career development opportunities, and engagement-fostering initiatives. This study contributes to the literature by empirically examining these integrated relationships within an understudied demographic and cultural context, while acknowledging limitations inherent in cross-sectional, self-report designs.

Through an empirical analysis of Japan's fiscal year 2026 budget of 122.3 trillion yen-whose core pillar is the 50% surge in the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) budget for AI and semiconductors-this paper reveals that sovereign credit is undergoing an "emergency reallocation" from fiat ledger entries to a physical computing power foundation. The study further defines the new social contract of "intellectual redemption" through the cases of "child investment accounts anchored in computing power assets" proposed in the United States and Taiwan, arguing that its essence is to prevent societal growing pains triggered by the AGI shock, rather than intergenerational wealth management in the traditional sense. Finally, drawing on the physical iron law of energy density and the productivity loop model, the paper systematically pronounces the logical death sentence on gold, Bitcoin, and bank-driven RWA (Real World Asset tokenization): the former degenerates into "civilization's ashes" due to its lack of logical increment and productivity empowerment; the latter becomes mere "ownerless dead code" in the face of computing power sovereignty due to its absence of physical defensive capacity. The paper concludes that, beginning in 2026, the credit formula has been thoroughly reconstructed as: Credit = Computing Power × Energy × Violence.

title: Employee Experience Capital and Organizational Performance: An Integrated Framework for Understanding Workplace Resource Systems in Digitally Transformed Organizations

detail.title: Employee Experience Capital and Organizational Performance: An Integrated Framework for Understanding Workplace Resource Systems in Digitally Transformed Organizations
detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations face the complex challenge of integrating diverse workplace resourcesspanning digital tools, inclusive practices, sustainability initiatives, and well-being programs-into coherent systems that simultaneously support employee flourishing and organizational effectiveness. This theoretical paper develops the concept of Employee Experience Capital (EEC), defined as the integrated configuration of organizational resources that shape employees' holistic work experiences and generate sustainable competitive advantage. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory and the Resource-Based View of the firm, this paper identifies seven illustrative dimensions of EEC-digital autonomy, psychological safety climate, sustainability alignment, human-AI collaboration, restorative work design, learning climate, and well-being support systems-and provides systematic theoretical justification for their selection based on Self-Determination Theory's basic psychological needs framework. The paper proposes that EEC influences organizational performance through two empirically distinguishable mediating pathways: work meaningfulness (a cognitive-evaluative pathway) and experienced vitality (an affectiveenergetic pathway). Specific propositions predict which EEC dimensions more strongly affect each pathway. The framework advances theory by demonstrating how ostensibly disparate organizational practices function as an integrated resource system with emergent properties. The paper acknowledges boundary conditions, engages with competing theoretical perspectives, and discusses potential tensions and dark sides of EEC dimensions. Implications for research methodology and organizational practice are discussed.

title: Transfer Pricing Compliance among Multinational Corporations in Developing Economies

detail.title: Transfer Pricing Compliance among Multinational Corporations in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Transfer pricing today is front and center for tax authorities in many developing countries and for good reason. It touches revenue collection, fairness in the tax system, and how governments regulate big multinational firms. As cross-border deals and intra-group transactions grow, gaps in transfer pricing compliance leave poorer countries particularly vulnerable to base erosion and profit shifting. This paper pulls together empirical studies, legal analyses, and policy work on the topic, with a clear bent toward issues faced by developing economies. What comes through, again and again, are persistent weaknesses: shaky enforcement, clever regulatory arbitrage by multinationals, a big information gap between taxpayers and tax authorities, and simply not enough administrative or technical muscle within revenue agencies. The review also flags a common problem: the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines are a useful global touchstone, sure, but they don't work like magic when you just copy them in without fitting them to local laws, institutions, and economic realities. The main takeaway? Leaning only on international standards won't fix these compliance problems. Instead, the study argues for a blended approach that includes regulatory reform plus beefed-up audit and admin capacity, clearer transparency tools, and stronger international cooperation for sharing information and providing technical help (Kalra and Afzal; Eukeria and Mpofu; Mashiri et al.; Pareno).

title: Sectoral Analysis of Transfer Pricing Risks in Extractive Industries

detail.title: Sectoral Analysis of Transfer Pricing Risks in Extractive Industries
detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine the risks associated with transfer pricing (TP) within Africa's and other emerging economies' extractive industries value chains. For this purpose, the study aimed to identify high-risk activities, compliance gaps, and distinct risks within the value chain. The study employed comparative analysis methodology, using an extensive review of secondary research data for the natural resource sectors, particularly for mining, oil, and gas industries. The findings indicate that the extractive industries value chain is particularly vulnerable to TP risks, considering that value chain players deal with numerous inter-company transactions, value (pricing) natural resources, and frequently grant or rely on associated party or related party financing. Default compliance, gaps of no or low legal enforcement, and the non-application or selective enforcement of the arm's length principle are among the explanatory factors that create an opportunity for profit and profit shifting or base erosion. The study also identifies the costs associated with and challenges posed by the pricing of mineral exports and services, the transfer of intangible assets, and the calculation of royalties. The study's findings provide the basis for suggesting a more focused and targeted set of policy alternatives, including the strengthening of regulatory frameworks, the establishment of more robust monitoring and auditing functionalities, and the development of targeted training and capacity-building programs for tax administrators. Effective risk mitigation strategies are also proposed, emphasizing the need for greater transparency, adherence to OECD guidelines, and adoption of advanced reporting mechanisms. By providing a structured understanding of TP risks in extractive sectors, this research contributes to informed policymaking, improved compliance, and sustainable revenue mobilization in emerging economies.

title: Challenges of Implementing BEPS in Low-Income Countries

detail.title: Challenges of Implementing BEPS in Low-Income Countries
detail.abstract: This study aims to explain the difficulties experienced when the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) framework is applied to low-income countries. In such countries, the lack of resources, difficulty of the cross-cutting tax systems, and problems within the tax administrative systems complicate the enforcement of the BEPS framework. Using country and regional BEPS reports in combination with relevant literature and case studies, I describe the structural, legal, and managerial complexities of the BEPS framework. I demonstrate that the BEPS framework is useful and adaptable to the contexts of low-income countries, but remains underutilized due to the lack of relevant expertise, poor regulatory environment, and the absence of congruent domestic laws (Schwarz 45; Shome 112). The absence of congruent domestic laws further complicates the low-income countries' context, as the BEPS framework is intended to soften the impact of a geographically remote digital economy, a situation where taxation becomes particularly difficult. In response to the problem of the non-aligning BEPS framework, this study argues for interventions of a policy nature, such as the establishment of operational and capacity-building partnerships, within the parameters of a relational policy framework, with international organizations. Policy implications indicate that the BEPS guidelines are too broad to be effective on their own. The author suggests that for BEPS to be effective, there must be enforcement mechanisms, tools for adapting to the context, and digital tax tools. The author clarifies the constraints and makes suggestions, so the author responds to the ambiguity in international tax governance with suggestions for developing countries to protect their revenue without hindering foreign direct investment (Oguttu 168).

title: Indoor Routing Optimization for School and Hospital Emergencies Using GIS Data

detail.title: Indoor Routing Optimization for School and Hospital Emergencies Using GIS Data
detail.abstract: The rural emergency response systems still suffer from serious issues caused by the remote location of sparsely populated rural areas, limited resources, and the legacy 911 system, which all promote slow response and poor emergency care access (Access to Emergency Care in Rural Illinois). The study uses previously collected response time data and efficiency benchmarks from emergency communication studies (Indoor Routing for School Emergencies; Alamri) for a comparative pre-and post-Next Generation 911 (NG911) analysis to determine the changes in call dispatch processing and routing precision to 1st responders and time to scene. The statistically significant evidence in dispatch and on-scene arrival time drops post NG911 implementation spearheaded by rural counties in the use of advanced geovisual data and communication interoperability (Han et al.; Guo and He). Yet, the extent of the performance improvement within the study was not consistent across the different implementation settings, which suggests that the general lack of positive rural emergency response system improvements cannot simply be attributed to the lack of technology in the system (Zverovich et al). A closer look shows that organizational readiness, inter-agency coordination, and the way people interact with technology, human technology interaction really shape how effective NG911-enabled systems are; they don't just matter a little, they significantly mediate outcomes, which underlines the need for holistic implementation strategies (Rodríguez-Espíndola et al.). Put another way (and to be honest, this feels important): NG911 should be thought of as an integrated socio-technical system, not a pile of tech you buy and hope for the best. Lasting improvements in rural emergency response depend on aligning infrastructure, governance, and everyday operational practices, rather than treating technology as a standalone fix (Zverovich et al.; Rodríguez-Espíndola et al.).

title: The Impact of English Language Skills on the Employee Performance

detail.title: The Impact of English Language Skills on the Employee Performance
detail.abstract: This study aims to find the relationship and impact of English language skills on employee performance. The English language skills, represented by its dimensions (listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills), are stated as the independent variable, while employee performance is the dependent variable. To address the study problem, three main hypotheses are proposed for testing. The research is divided into two parts. The first part involves discussing the theoretical aspects related to the study variables. The second part represents the field aspect of the study, where the causal relationship between the study variables in the Directorate of Relations of the studied universities is examined. The sample consists of 14 Directorates of Relations/ public universities, where the questionnaire form was distributed randomly using Google Form, with a total of (102) forms distributed and (95) valid forms collected for analysis. After entering the collected data from the sample respondents' questionnaire answers into the statistical analysis program (SPSS v.26), a set of findings was obtained. The most significant finding is the presence of a strong significant correlation between the variables and their dimensions at both the overall and partial levels. The correlation coefficients are high, confirming a strong association between the variables. The results also confirm a significant impact of English language skills at the general level, indicating the researched universities' interest in practicing the dimensions of English language skills (listening, speaking, reading, and writing) for better employee performance. Based on the results, the researcher presents a set of suggestions, the most important of which is the necessity for universities to prioritize their employees by providing them with training courses to enhance their language skills, especially in English, to strengthen relationships with other IX international universities and establish a culture of English language skills within the Directorate of Relations of the participated universities. This should be embraced by employees and reflected in their behavior and knowledge to improve their performance efficiency. The study concludes with a set of future research suggestions to assist researchers in conducting research and studies related to the current study variables.

title: The Psychology of Exceptional Achievement: An Integrative Framework for Understanding the Genesis of Great Work

detail.title: The Psychology of Exceptional Achievement: An Integrative Framework for Understanding the Genesis of Great Work
detail.abstract: What psychological and behavioral factors distinguish those who produce exceptional, original contributions from those who achieve competence without breakthrough impact? This article synthesizes research from cognitive psychology, motivation science, expertise studies, and the sociology of knowledge to propose an integrative framework for understanding exceptional achievement. Drawing on both empirical research and theoretical analysis, the paper identifies four sequential phases through which great work emerges-domain selection, frontier attainment, gap identification, and persistent exploration-and examines three enabling conditions that sustain the process: deep curiosity, earnest engagement, and resilient morale. The framework reconciles deliberate practice models with creativity research, addresses the role of social and institutional factors, and offers implications for education, mentorship, and self-directed development. The analysis suggests that exceptional achievement, while rare, follows discernible patterns that can inform both individual practice and institutional design.

title: The Burden of Knowledge and the Changing Landscape of Innovation: A Critical Analysis of Age and Great Invention

detail.title: The Burden of Knowledge and the Changing Landscape of Innovation: A Critical Analysis of Age and Great Invention
detail.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive critical analysis of Benjamin F. Jones's influential work on age and great invention, which documents a significant secular trend toward older ages at which inventors make breakthrough contributions. Drawing on data from Nobel Prize winners and great inventors across the twentieth century, Jones finds that the mean age at great invention increased by approximately six years over this period, attributing this shift to the expanding "burden of knowledge." This article examines Jones's theoretical framework, empirical methodology, and the broader implications of his findings for innovation policy and economic growth. While acknowledging the paper's substantial contributions, this analysis identifies important limitations-including concerns about measurement validity, alternative causal interpretations, and the generalizability of findings-and engages with contradictory evidence that complicates the burden of knowledge narrative. The article situates Jones's work within broader literatures spanning economics, psychology, and the sociology of science, ultimately arguing that while the burden of knowledge hypothesis offers a compelling partial explanation for observed trends, the phenomenon is likely more complex and contingent than the original framework suggests.

title: Impact of Real-Time GIS Data on First Responder Decision-Making During Disasters

detail.title: Impact of Real-Time GIS Data on First Responder Decision-Making During Disasters
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of real-time GIS data on the decision-making of first responders in disaster situations, in particular, the challenges of operating in dynamic, high-uncertainty situations. The paper engages in conceptual and comparative analyses of GIS-enabled systems for emergency and comparative systems, and deals with real-time systems in emergency response, Next Generation 911 (NG911) systems, indoor routing systems, smart city GIS systems, and real-time spatial analytics. The analysis assesses the emergency response systems in each area to determine how real-time spatial data is created, assimilated, and utilized in management systems. The data shows that emergency responders' real-time GIS systems help them understand and respond to situations better because they provide data that represent the location and movement of hazards, resources, and people, and that the systems' speed of response and accuracy of tracking routes via dynamic routing and outdoor-to-indoor navigation (Mbuh et al.; Kwan and Lee; Hao and Wang; NG911 studies) improves. Improvements in decision quality are particularly visible when GIS in real time is combined with specific responder training, specific frameworks of standardised data, and cross-agency interoperability. The study highlights the importance of real-time GIS data in contemporary disaster response. It shifts the focus of real-time GIS data from being seen as a simple technological resource to being a vital decision support infrastructural resource. This is why the integration of real-time GIS, along with governance and the development of workforce capacity, needs to be prioritised in emergency planning and policy.

detail.abstract:
This conceptual essay proposes Conscious Libertarianism as an adaptive economic framework grounded in human behavior, evolutionary incentives, and decentralized competition. Departing from rigid libertarian formulations, the framework integrates insights from classical liberalism, Austrian economics, and evolutionary theory to examine how wealth, institutions, and ideas emerge, adapt, or disappear through market-based selection mechanisms. The analysis emphasizes rational self-interest, consumer-driven selection, and competitive responsibility as emergent forces capable of generating genuine wealth creation rather than mere transactional growth.

Rather than advancing a prescriptive policy model, this work presents an exploratory structure intentionally exposed to intellectual competition. Firms, labor arrangements, monetary institutions, and the framework itself are analyzed as evolutionary entities subject to adaptation and failure. Particular attention is given to the role of the conscious consumer as an active architect of economic evolution, exerting selective pressure on enterprises through decentralized decision-making. The essay concludes by positioning publication as an evolutionary step, allowing criticism to function as a mechanism of theoretical selection and refinement.

title: Comparative Study of OECD vs Non-OECD Transfer Pricing Regulations
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Comparative Study of OECD vs Non-OECD Transfer Pricing Regulations
detail.abstract: This study examines and compares transfer pricing regulations in OECD and non-OECD countries to identify key differences in compliance frameworks and their implications for multinational enterprises (MNEs). A comparative methodology was employed, incorporating a systematic literature review, analysis of relevant case studies, and evaluation of statistical data on regulatory enforcement and corporate compliance. The findings indicate that OECD countries largely adhere to standardized transfer pricing guidelines, emphasizing documentation requirements, arm's-length principles, and structured dispute resolution mechanisms. In contrast, non-OECD jurisdictions exhibit considerable variability in their regulatory approaches, ranging from loosely defined rules to country-specific mandates that often diverge from international norms. These differences have tangible impacts on MNEs, influencing compliance costs, risk exposure, and strategic tax planning. The study also reveals that enforcement effectiveness is generally higher in OECD countries due to clearer regulatory frameworks and coordinated international oversight, whereas non-OECD countries face challenges such as limited administrative capacity and inconsistent implementation. Overall, while OECD guidelines offer coherent global direction and facilitate cross-border predictability, the heterogeneity of non-OECD regulations introduces complexity and uncertainty for multinational operations. The study underscores the importance of MNEs adopting adaptive compliance strategies that account for both global standards and local regulatory nuances. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of the international transfer pricing landscape and highlight areas for potential harmonization and policy improvement.

title: How Much to Sell versus Store? Strategic Production Allocation under Post-Harvest Loss and Storage Constraints
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Indore and Indian Institute of Management Indore

detail.title: How Much to Sell versus Store? Strategic Production Allocation under Post-Harvest Loss and Storage Constraints
detail.abstract: This study examines the strategic trade-offs faced by small and marginal farmers in allocating agricultural produce between two selling channels. When farmers sell their produce in the open market, they often incur post-harvest losses due to inadequate storage infrastructure, poor material handling, and limited transportation facilities, which can result in distress sales of perishable goods. Alternatively, participation in cold storage-either through investment or rental-introduces challenges in the form of high fixed costs and uncertainty about future retail prices due to agricultural price volatility. To analyze these trade-offs, we develop a multi-stage game-theoretic model with two selling channels: an open market that operates as a competitive channel and cold storage that functions as a cooperative channel. We characterize farmers' equilibrium production decisions and derive the optimal cost-sharing and allocation outcomes under Nash bargaining when future retail prices are based on farmers' price estimates. We show that a farmer's cost-sharing burden decreases when the other farmer possesses better price information. Moreover, when cold storage capacity is limited, a farmer with lower bargaining power is forced to sell a positive quantity in the open market. Regardless of bargaining power, allocating the entire output to the open market is never optimal for farmers. We further extend the analysis to incorporate a government cold storage subsidy scheme and examine its spillover effects on farmers' profits. Our results show that the subsidy scheme is social welfare improving, while imbalanced bargaining power among farmers leads to inferior system-wide outcomes.

title: Forecasting the U.S. Treasury Yield Curve: A Distributionally Robust Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: and Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU)

detail.title: Forecasting the U.S. Treasury Yield Curve: A Distributionally Robust Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Global asset prices are interconnected through sovereign bond yield curve dynamics, with U.S. Treasuries serving as the benchmark for global interest-rate pricing. Even for U.S. Treasuries-the most liquid and data-dependent fixed-income instruments-yields are noisy and shaped by policy communication, evolving supply-demand conditions, and behavioral forces. In such environments, forecast users face material downside risk when making decisions under policy uncertainty and market stress. We study U.S. Treasury yield curve forecasting under distributional uncertainty and recast forecasting as an operations-research and managerial decision problem in which the forecaster selects a rule to minimize worst-case expected loss over admissible forecast-error distributions. We propose a distributionally robust ensemble forecasting framework that integrates parametric factor models with high-dimensional nonparametric machine learning models through adaptive forecast combinations. The framework has three ML/AI components. A rolling-window Factor-Augmented Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (FADNS) model captures level, slope, and curvature dynamics using principal components from economic indicators. Random Forest models capture nonlinear interactions among economic drivers and lagged Treasury yields. Distributionally robust forecast-combination schemes aggregate heterogeneous forecasts under moment uncertainty, penalizing downside tail risk via expected shortfall and stabilizing second-moment estimation through ridge-regularized covariance matrices. The severity of the worst-case criterion is adjustable, allowing the forecaster to regulate robustness against forecast errors. Using monthly data, we evaluate out-of-sample forecasts across maturities and horizons from one to twelve months ahead. Adaptive combinations outperform at short horizons, while Random Forest forecasts dominate at longer horizons. Extensions to global sovereign bond yields confirm the stability and generalizability of the proposed framework.

title: The Power of Belonging: Confirmatory Factor Analysis of the Belonging Barometer with Child Welfare Workers
