detail.abstract: The AI-Powered Music Recommendation System is an intelligent and scalable platform designed to enhance the music listening experience by delivering personalized song recommendations using advanced artificial intelligence techniques. By integrating machine learning-based recommendation algorithms with audio feature analysis and user behaviour modelling, the system analyses user preferences, listening history, ratings, moods, and interaction patterns to generate accurate and relevant music suggestions. Unlike traditional music recommendation approaches that rely primarily on popularity trends or static playlists, this system effectively handles diverse music genres, evolving user tastes, and large-scale music datasets with improved precision and adaptability. The recommendation engine utilizes collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and hybrid techniques to ensure high-quality and context-aware recommendations. The system provides an interactive user interface that allows listeners to search, browse, play music, and receive real-time personalized recommendations, while administrators can efficiently manage songs, users, playlists, and analytical reports. Additionally, the platform incorporates feedback mechanisms and learning modules that continuously improve recommendation accuracy based on user interactions.

detail.title: International Journal of Production Research
detail.abstract: This study investigates blockchain's effectiveness and the drivers of its success in supply chain management. Drawing upon the Information Systems Success post-adoption model and Contingency Theory, we propose a moderated mediation analysis to analyze the relationships among extended use, user satisfaction, individual benefits, supply chain complexity, and their impact on performance outcomes at both the supply chain and individual firm levels. The model was validated by using survey data from a cross-sectional sample of 370 supply chain professionals from the United States with blockchain experience. Our findings indicate that individual benefits mediate the impact of extended use and user satisfaction on supply chain and operational performance, while supply chain complexity positively moderates the indirect effect of extended use on supply chain performance through individual benefits. This suggests that blockchain adoption is more impactful in complex supply chain contexts with numerous processes, stakeholders, and data sources. These results highlight the importance of adequately considering the supply chain context to fully understand the effectiveness of blockchain technology. This study contributes to the nascent literature on the blockchain post-adoption phase and proposes a new extension to the Information Systems Success model by incorporating supply chain complexity as a contextual factor.

title: Asymmetric Compliance: Behavioral Intent vs. Systemic Friction in the Era of AI-Driven IRS Collections

detail.title: Asymmetric Compliance: Behavioral Intent vs. Systemic Friction in the Era of AI-Driven IRS Collections
detail.abstract: This research examines how "administrative attrition" at the Internal Revenue Service-driven by historical mail backlogs, funding volatility, and the forced retirement of senior personnel-has created a systemic environment where taxpayer "innocence" is increasingly difficult to prove. While the Service has prioritized AI-driven data matching through FATCA, its "analog" infrastructure remains paralyzed by political volatility and archaic processing systems. This paper argues that "systemic friction" (delayed notices, processing backlogs, and asynchronous communication) often mimics the markers of willful non-compliance. By analyzing TIGTA reporting on historical processing failures and current lapses in appropriations, this research provides defense counsel with a behavioral framework to establish Reasonable Cause under 26 U.S.C. § 6664.

title: Not Just a Transition

detail.title: Not Just a Transition
detail.abstract: To meet the targets of the Paris Agreement, coal must be phased out urgently across the world. To support low- and middle-income countries in phasing out coal, various countries, including South Africa, have signed Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETPs) with a group of developed countries, including the US, the UK, Germany and others. Yet, little is known about the effectiveness of JETPs in phasing down coal investments. This paper examines the stock price reaction of South African coal mining companies to the announcement of the South African JETP at COP26. Our findings indicate a significant decline in coal company valuations, suggesting that investors perceive the JETP as a credible threat to coal profitability and are factoring in the risk of stranded assets. These results are further supported by evidence from international coal markets, where futures prices also exhibited large and statistically significant declines.

title: Advancing Seismic Capacity Curve Predictions with A Meta-modeling Framework for Structural Systems
affiliations: and Oregon State University

detail.title: Advancing Seismic Capacity Curve Predictions with A Meta-modeling Framework for Structural Systems
detail.abstract: Predicting accurate seismic capacity curves for reinforced concrete (RC) bridges is essential for assessing seismic performance and resilience, particularly in earthquake-prone regions such as the Pacific Northwest. The Cascadia Subduction Zone megathrust earthquake presents a critical threat to such infrastructure, yet traditional approaches often fail to capture the nonlinearities and high-dimensional relationships between structural parameters and seismic responses. While single-model machine learning (ML) techniques have shown promise, their limited robustness and generalizability hinder their effectiveness. To address these challenges, this research introduces a stacked machine learning framework to enhance the prediction of capacity curves, specifically using column drift ratios as a key measure of structural performance under seismic loading. The proposed framework systematically evaluates various regression models to construct an optimized meta-model by selecting the bestperforming algorithms based on predictive accuracy and generalizability. Incremental Dynamic Analysis (IDA) is performed on randomized RC bridge samples, with input parameters systematically varied using the Latin Hypercube Sampling technique to generate a diverse training dataset. Ground motion suites tailored to Cascadia-specific long-duration seismic characteristics ensure the framework's regional applicability. Advanced ensemble and boostingbased regression algorithms, such as Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are tested and the top-performing models are combined into the meta-model. This stacked approach addresses the limitations of single-model techniques by improving robustness, accuracy, and the ability to generalize across diverse structural configurations. The ML models predict capacity curves based on column drift ratios, providing precise and actionable insights into structural performance. To ensure interpretability, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), are used to rank the importance of input parameters, offering actionable insights for seismic design and retrofit strategies. This stacked machine learning approach offers several advantages, including the ability to model complex, nonlinear relationships and produce accurate capacity curve predictions for RC bridges. Results demonstrate that the framework enhances the reliability of seismic risk assessments and reduces computational demands, empowering engineers and decision-makers to design, evaluate, and retrofit infrastructure with greater confidence. By overcoming the limitations of existing methodologies, this research highlights the transformative potential of stacked machine learning in advancing seismic risk assessment practices and strengthening infrastructure resilience.

title: Trinity Law Framework: Health Insurance Taxonomy

detail.title: Trinity Law Framework: Health Insurance Taxonomy

detail.abstract: Definition Despite seven decades of international commitment-from the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights through SDG 3.8-universal health coverage remains stubbornly out of reach. Two billion people, predominantly informal sector workers, lack access to sustainable health insurance. This entry explains the underlying cause: sustainable health insurance requires specific behavioral and institutional conditions for collective action-conditions that existing health insurance models systematically fail to satisfy, thereby structurally excluding informal populations. The Trinity Law framework formalizes these conditions as three multiplicatively interacting requirements-Trust (T), Consensus (C), and Dual Benefit (DB)-expressed as S = T × C × DB. Empirical analysis of community-based health insurance schemes across 24 countries identifies a robust trust threshold (τ* ≈ 0.68) operating as a behavioral phase transition: below this level, cooperation collapses; above it, participation becomes self-sustaining. Crosscountry evidence from 274 organizations across 155 countries confirms consensus thresholds (C* ≈ 0.59), while analysis of 158,763 observations validates dual benefit mechanisms. The multiplicative structure explains why partial reforms fail: weakness in any single component drives overall sustainability toward zero. Applied to health insurance, this framework distinguishes conventional systems-Bismarckian employment-based, Beveridgean tax-financed, and commercial health insurance from sustainable systems like participatory community-based microinsurance that satisfy all three Trinity Law conditions through participatory design, transparent governance, and aligned incentives. The persistent UHC gap reflects not implementation failures but fundamental design incompatibilities that the Trinity Law makes explicit. This entry has three objectives: first, it states the Trinity Law conditions; second, it summarizes the empirical evidence for each component; third, it applies the framework to classify major health insurance models. Supporting datasets and code are available in the referenced Zenodo repositories. The term 'law' follows the tradition of social science regularities like the 'law of demand': a robust empirical pattern with strong predictive validity, not a claim to physical certainty.

title: Algorithmic Pricing Manipulation

detail.title: Algorithmic Pricing Manipulation
detail.abstract: Algorithmic pricing is now ubiquitous. Markets often contain firms using simple rule-based heuristics and firms using reinforcement learning (RL). I study such mixed environments and show that RL agents systematically manipulate widely used profit-and sales-based rules. In a Bertrand-Logit setting with discrete price grids, I simulate Q-learning and deep RL (DRL) agents playing against wincontinue lose-reverse (WCLR) and other profit-and sales-based pricing (PBSB) rules. The RL agents learn policies that push PBSB rivals to the top of the grid while keeping their own prices low, raising rivals' prices and the RL agents' profits. When multiple RL firms play against PBSB rivals, the RL firms coordinate with each other on a collusive manipulation and impose punishments after deviations. I show that the learned RL policies are typically Nash equilibria. Manipulation is very robust to increasing the number of PBSB rivals in the setting, but it weakens when the number of RL firms increases.

title: The Structural Knot: A Conceptual Framework for Irreversible Decision Thresholds

detail.title: The Structural Knot: A Conceptual Framework for Irreversible Decision Thresholds
detail.abstract: Contemporary decision-making models predominantly rely on optimization, bounded rationality, or bias-correction frameworks. These approaches implicitly assume reversibility, iterative adjustment, or the possibility of delegation. However, certain human decisions occur under conditions where these assumptions no longer hold. This paper introduces the Knot, a minimal conceptual framework describing a structural threshold beyond which a decision becomes irreversible prior to any observable execution. The Knot is neither a predictive model nor a prescriptive tool; it functions as an observational structure allowing the identification of moments in which decision-making shifts from optimization to commitment. The framework emphasizes structural constraint, internal engagement, and temporal asymmetry. Inspired by historical observational methodologies rather than instrumental modeling, the paper integrates schematic, anatomical-style drawings as epistemic instruments intended to constrain observation rather than to explain a mechanism. Situated within the broader field of structural thresholds, the Knot provides a non-normative framework applicable to the analysis of leadership, ethical decision-making, crisis contexts, and human-AI interaction, while explicitly acknowledging its conceptual limits.

detail.abstract: The integration of fiscal and monetary policies is critical for achieving macroeconomic stability, particularly in developing countries. This study introduces a novel framework, the Economic Policy Integration Index (EPII), designed to quantitatively assess the degree of coordination between fiscal and monetary policies. By applying the EPII model to Egypt, Turkey, and Morocco, this research evaluates the effectiveness of policy synchronization and identifies areas for improvement. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers seeking to enhance economic stability through coordinated policy measures .

title: Decoding the Beige Book: LLM-Powered Sentiment Analysis for Real-Time Recession Forecasting

detail.title: Decoding the Beige Book: LLM-Powered Sentiment Analysis for Real-Time Recession Forecasting
detail.abstract: In this research, we apply large language models (LLMs) to systematically analyze the sentiment contained in the Federal Reserve's Beige Book, a key qualitative resource to evaluate U.S. macroeconomic conditions. Leveraging both general-purpose and financespecific LLMs, we developed an automated pipeline to extract topiclevel sentiment scores from over five decades of Beige Book reports. We compare national and district-level sentiment signals, benchmark multiple LLMs, and quantify the predictive power of different economic topics for recession risk across various forecast horizons. Sentiments generated by multiple LLM models are able to confident signals for recession nowcasting, with peak performance at the contemporaneous horizon (F1 scores up to 0.89). By combining LLMs and structured sentiment analysis, we see the potential for AI-powered sentiment analysis to supplement traditional macroeconomic indicators in predicting recession risks.

detail.abstract: Rural and underserved school districts across the United States continue to face persistent literacy gaps that undermine educational equity, workforce readiness, and long-term economic mobility. These disparities are driven by a complex interaction of structural, geographic, economic, and technological factors, including limited instructional resources, teacher shortages, constrained funding, and uneven access to digital infrastructure. Because literacy proficiency underpins academic success across all subject areas, persistent rural literacy gaps represent an issue of national importance with implications for workforce development, civic participation, and social mobility. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), offer new opportunities to support literacy development through adaptive instruction, automated feedback, and scalable access to high-quality learning materials. LLMs have demonstrated the ability to generate context-aware explanations, model reading and writing strategies, assist with vocabulary development, and support differentiated instruction. Despite this potential, adoption of LLMs in rural public education systems remains limited. Barriers include concerns regarding student data privacy, algorithmic bias, infrastructure readiness, educator trust, cost, and the absence of governance-aligned implementation frameworks. This manuscript presents a full-length, conceptual framework for deploying LLMs to enhance literacy outcomes in underserved rural U.S. school districts. The framework emphasizes systemlevel integration with existing education information systems, educator-centered oversight, explainability, and compliance with public-sector governance requirements such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA). Rather than positioning LLMs as autonomous instructional agents, the proposed approach frames them as decision-support and instructional augmentation tools that strengthen teacher capacity and expand equitable access to literacy support. By focusing on literacy as a foundational educational outcome, this paper contributes to scholarship on artificial intelligence in education, rural education policy, and digital equity. The framework offers actionable guidance for policymakers, administrators, and education technology leaders seeking to reduce rural achievement gaps through responsible, scalable, and sustainable AI adoption.

title: Startup Legal from the Inside Out: A Practical Guide to Building a Legal Function that Scales

detail.title: Startup Legal from the Inside Out: A Practical Guide to Building a Legal Function that Scales
detail.abstract:
This book began with a persistent observation: legal tends to arrive late in startups, often stepping in only after the consequences of its absence have already caused disruption or damage. I have witnessed this pattern repeatedly. Founders with vision, operators with precision, and technologists with extraordinary creativity build exceptional products and businesses yet leave legal frameworks and safeguards behind in the name of urgency.

This delay is rarely the result of carelessness. More often, it stems from the intense pressure to move quickly, capture opportunities, and maintain momentum in a competitive market. In such a high-velocity environment, legal is too often perceived as nonessential—until a poorly structured contract jeopardizes a partnership, an unassigned intellectual property right blocks a product launch, or a missed compliance step stalls a funding round. These failures are not reflections of insufficient talent or ambition but of systems never properly designed to support long-term growth. And, in most cases, the resulting problems could have been prevented.

Over the years, I have had the privilege of working alongside startups across multiple sectors and stages, frequently stepping in as the first internal legal advisor. In that role, I have partnered with product teams deciding when to launch, supported finance departments navigating term sheets, and advised founders facing difficult choices during international expansion or organizational restructuring. In each of those situations, legal was not present to impede progress but to enable informed decisions, bring clarity to ambiguity, and provide the necessary structure to move forward with integrity.

The need for this book arises from the reality that too many early-stage companies still operate without a legal function that is properly integrated into their core decision making. Many legal professionals entering the startup environment find themselves overwhelmed, isolated, or under-resourced. Founders often continue to regard legal as a reactive expense rather than a proactive contributor. And across departments, business teams regularly encounter legal issues without the guidance or confidence to address them effectively.

This book is intended to meet the needs of multiple readers. For founders seeking to build sustainable companies, it offers a roadmap for embedding legal early and scaling it intelligently. For legal professionals establishing the function from within, it provides frameworks, workflows, and communication strategies suited to a fast-paced environment. For operational leaders, product managers, HR professionals, and finance teams who routinely make decisions with legal implications, it offers clarity and actionable resources designed to reduce uncertainty and prevent rework.

detail.abstract: Gold and technology stocks are traditionally viewed as moving in opposite directions-gold as a defensive asset and technology equities as growth-oriented investments. However, recent market behavior shows sustained periods in which both assets rise simultaneously. This paper investigates why this apparent contradiction occurs by analyzing historical market data under similar macroeconomic conditions. Instead of assuming a fixed relationship between assets, the study compares periods with comparable inflation, interest rates, currency strength, and market volatility. The results show that gold and technology stocks can and often do move together under specific economic regimes, particularly those characterized by low real interest rates and elevated uncertainty.

title: Runtime Autonomy Oversight (RAO): A Governance Framework for Scalable Physical Autonomy

detail.title: Runtime Autonomy Oversight (RAO): A Governance Framework for Scalable Physical Autonomy
detail.abstract: Autonomous physical systems, including humanoid robots, mobile robots, automated warehouses, and other forms of physical AI, are rapidly advancing in capability and deployment scale. However, widespread adoption remains constrained by operational instability, concentrated liability, and uncertainty around insurability and accountability. These constraints do not primarily stem from failures in perception, planning, or control. Instead, they arise from system-level behavior under uncertainty, particularly when autonomous agents interact with dynamic environments, degraded sensing, and one another. This paper introduces Runtime Autonomy Oversight (RAO), a governance framework that regulates autonomous physical systems while they are operating, rather than relying solely on design-time policies, static safety rules, or post-incident analysis. RAO enables Governed Autonomy through two core artifacts: the Autonomy State Ledger and the Risk Modulation Envelope. Together, these mechanisms establish a practical, auditable foundation for safe, insurable, and scalable physical autonomy.

detail.abstract: This chapter reconceptualizes reparations for Black Americans as a contractual remedy for the breach of emancipation, reframing redress not as a moral or political gesture but as the expectation damages owed under American contract law. Against a backdrop of judicial hostility to affirmative action and the political rollback of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, it introduces the American Reparations Trust-a lineage-based, privately funded vehicle for reparative justice. Modeled after quasi-public financial entities and sustained by corporate tax incentives, the Trust bypasses constitutional and legislative barriers to offer a scalable, market-aligned path toward redress. It draws on theories of racial capitalism and structural exclusion to argue that private actors who benefited from slavery and its afterlives now bear the obligation to perform where the state has failed. In so doing, the chapter proposes a pragmatic legal infrastructure for reparations rooted in the logic of performance, not apology.

detail.abstract: We analyze how economic sanctions reshape oil trade flows using monthly seaborne crude export data for Venezuela from January 2022 to December 2025. The data reveal three distinct adjustment phases: an extreme concentration toward China during 2022-2023, a partial rediversification with renewed U.S.-bound exports in 2024, and a sharp increase in opaque routing at the end of 2025. Rather than eliminating exports, sanctions alter trade geography, increase information frictions, and generate new strategic dependencies in global oil markets.

detail.abstract: We examine the impact of top-of-screen promotions on viewing time at ABEMA, a leading video streaming platform in Japan. Notably, promoting short content proves most effective in that it not only retains users but also motivates them to watch subsequent episodes.

detail.abstract: This study aims to explore the relationship between marketing strategies and purchasing decisions based on the 4P marketing mix in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), with the research subject being used car showrooms in the Indonesian context. The research design adopted a quantitative method operationalized with an explanatory survey. The survey was conducted by distributing research questionnaires to 95 respondents selected using a combination of purposive and convenience sampling techniques. The data analysis and estimation method used a multiple linear regression model estimated using SPSS v.27. The results showed that product, price, place, and promotion have a positive and significant influence on purchasing decisions, both partially and simultaneously. Product, price, place, and promotion together can explain variance in purchasing decisions, with strong predictive power. This finding can fill the existing gap, where the traditional 4P marketing mix model is still relevant to be developed in implementing marketing strategies in the era of digital disruption in the 21 st century, by combining product, price, place or distribution strategies and promotional strategies that have been effectively carried out by used car sales showrooms as a marketing strategy that can influence consumer purchasing decisions. Marketing strategy implementation has been shown to have significant potential to be more targeted in increasing customer engagement and consumer purchasing decisions by integrating the 4Ps marketing mix components into the marketing strategies in the AI era.This research expands the literature in marketing management, specifically on marketing strategy, the relevance of the traditional 4Ps marketing mix and its evolution, and their combination in influencing purchase intentions and purchasing decisions. This can be adopted and developed in marketing practices across various companies, both conventional and digital. The presence of AI facilitates marketers' need to direct and develop marketing strategies and marketing mix instruments that are more attractive to target markets amidst the challenges of competition in the digital age. A visualization of the model that links marketing strategy with purchasing decisions through the 4P marketing mix model in the era of AI disruption is presented at the end of this paper.

title: SANOS (Smooth strictly Arbitrage-free Non-parametric Option Surfaces)
affiliations: , University of Oxford, McMaster University, University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance and University of Toronto - Department of Computer Science

detail.title: SANOS (Smooth strictly Arbitrage-free Non-parametric Option Surfaces)
detail.abstract:
We present a simple, numerically efficient and highly flexible non-parametric method to construct representations of option price surfaces which are both smooth and strictly arbitrage-free across time and strike. The method can be viewed as a smooth generalization of the widely-known linear interpolation scheme, and retains the simplicity and transparency of that baseline. 

Calibration of the model to observed market quotes is formulated as a linear program, allowing bid-ask spreads to be incorporated directly via linear penalties or inequalities, and delivering materially lower computational cost than most of the currently available implied-volatility surface fitting routines.

As a further contribution, we derive an equivalent parameterization of the proposed surface in terms of strictly positive "discrete local volatility" variables. This yields, to our knowledge, the first construction of smooth, strictly arbitrage-free option price surfaces while requiring only trivial parameter constraints (positivity). We illustrate the approach using S&P 500 index options.

detail.abstract: Education reforms remain a crucial cornerstone for sustaining quality education globally. Since the creation of Delta State in 1991, the Delta State government has implemented numerous reforms, such as free primary and secondary education and the introduction of education marshals, to solidify and maintain high-quality secondary education. This study investigated and evaluated the effectiveness of these reforms in improving the quality of secondary education in Delta State. Designed as a qualitative desk research that relied on the documentary method of data collection and analysis, the study utilised Deming's System of Profound Knowledge Theory as its theoretical framework. Findings reveal that key challenges persist despite many reforms, including persistently high illiteracy rates, declining student enrolment, prevalent student and teacher truancy, and absenteeism. title: The Impact of Perceived Cybersecurity Risks on Consumer Trust in Digital Banking Initiatives: A Robust Analysis of the 'MyAccount' Project in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq

detail.title: The Impact of Perceived Cybersecurity Risks on Consumer Trust in Digital Banking Initiatives: A Robust Analysis of the 'MyAccount' Project in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq
detail.abstract: The transition from cash-based economies to digital payroll systems, specifically the Kurdistan Regional Government's "MyAccount" (Hajmara Min) initiative, faces significant behavioral resistance rooted in security skepticism. This study empirically examines the determinants of consumer trust in digital banking, focusing on the trade-off between cybersecurity assurance and service convenience. Drawing on a robust dataset of 1,000 participants, the research employs quantitative analysis to validate the relationship between perceived risk and financial behavior. The findings substantiate a pervasive security anxiety among the population (Mean = 3.72/5), with a decisive 51% majority identifying "strong security protocols" as the primary prerequisite for adoption, significantly outweighing demand for customer service speed. Furthermore, the data reveals a statistically significant negative correlation (r =-0.37) between social influence and the preference for "cash hoarding," indicating that community endorsement is a more effective mechanism for reducing home-cash storage than technical features alone. Additionally, 66.5% of respondents demonstrated a willingness to trade user experience friction for security via Two-Factor Authentication (2FA). These results provide conclusive evidence that trust in the Iraqi banking sector is functionally dependent on visible cybersecurity guarantees rather than operational efficiency.

title: Beyond Ideology: Reclaiming Evidence-Based Discourse on Sex Work Policy - A Reflection on the Need for Intellectual Humility, Empirical Rigor, and Malasakit
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beyond Ideology: Reclaiming Evidence-Based Discourse on Sex Work Policy - A Reflection on the Need for Intellectual Humility, Empirical Rigor, and Malasakit
detail.abstract:
Public policy debates on pornography and sex work are increasingly shaped by ideologically entrenched positions that privilege moral certainty over empirical adequacy. Prohibitionist, libertarian, and religiously conservative frameworks—despite their normative differences—exhibit a shared methodological failure: the tendency to begin with predetermined conclusions and selectively marshal evidence in their support. This pattern of motivated reasoning distorts analysis, produces ineffective or harmful policy, and marginalizes the lived experiences of those most affected.

This essay argues for a reorientation of sex work policy discourse grounded in three principles: intellectual humility, empirical rigor, and malasakit (empathetic solicitude toward affected persons). Drawing on comparative policy research and empirical findings across jurisdictions, it demonstrates how criminalization and stigma are consistently associated with increased harm, while working conditions, labor protections, and harm-reduction approaches more reliably predict welfare outcomes. Central to this analysis is the recognition of heterogeneity in sex work experiences, which resists both universalizing narratives of victimhood and uncritical claims of empowerment.

Rather than advancing a definitive moral judgment on sex work, the essay insists on epistemic discipline in policy analysis: distinguishing normative commitments from empirical claims, applying consistent standards of evidence, and prioritizing measurable outcomes over ideological coherence. By exposing how moral certainty masquerades as analytical rigor, this work contributes to broader debates on evidence-based policymaking in contested social domains and offers a framework for policy discourse that is both empirically grounded and ethically attentive.

detail.abstract:
Fire and rehire has become a significant issue, especially in recent times, during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. This report dissects the practice of "fire and rehire" within the UK employment law framework, focusing on its increased popularity, ethical concerns, and possible claims that an employer may face.

Starting with a brief introduction of what fire and rehire is and why it is used, this report covers the legal context of fire and rehire, including key statutes such as the recent Code of Practice (Dismissal and Re-engagement) Order, 2024, TULRCA 1992, TUPE Regulations 2006, and the Employment Rights Act 1996. The dissertation further traces the historical evolution of the practice, with a focus on notable case law and its implications for employment relations.

In addition, we examine the socio-economic drivers behind the use of fire and rehire, as well as the potential legal claims employees can pursue, such as wrongful and unfair dismissal. It also discusses the role of trade unions, the effectiveness of current regulations, and the ongoing political debate surrounding the practice.

The report ultimately assesses whether fire and rehire is a necessary tool for business survival or an exploitative tactic that undermines workers' rights. It offers recommendations for future legal and policy reforms to better balance business flexibility with employee protection.

title: Carbon Emissions and Corporate Performance in an Emerging Market: Evidence from Thailand
affiliations: Thammasat University, Heriot-Watt University and Thammasat University

detail.title: Carbon Emissions and Corporate Performance in an Emerging Market: Evidence from Thailand
detail.abstract: This paper examines the financial relevance of corporate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions for Thai listed firms during 2022-2024, a critical period of intensified transition risks and disclosure mandates. Using firm-reported total GHG emissions matched to firm financials, we first document that emissions are highly concentrated: a small set of issuers accounts for a disproportionate share of aggregate emissions, implying that financed-emissions exposure can be reduced efficiently through targeted engagement and reallocation toward the largest contributors. We then estimate pooled panel regressions with year and sector fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors, relating profitability (ROA, ROE) and valuation (Tobin's Q) to log emissions, firm size, and controls, while allowing the emissions association to vary with market capitalization via a centered interaction. Across outcomes, higher emissions are associated with weaker firm performance and lower valuation; in the baseline specification, the coefficient on log(GHG) is negative and statistically significant for ROA, ROE, and Tobin's Q. Results are similar when emissions are lagged by one year, and economic-magnitude calculations indicate that a 10% increase in emissions corresponds to modest declines in accounting profitability but a more noticeable reduction in Tobin's Q, consistent with markets pricing expected transition costs before they fully materialize in contemporaneous earnings. At the same time, causality-oriented diagnostics show that past performance predicts subsequent emissions and that future emissions predict current outcomes, highlighting that the estimates should be interpreted as conditional correlations rather than causal effects. Overall, the evidence suggests that emissions measures carry information relevant to valuation and risk assessment in the Thai equity market and provides practical guidance for investor stewardship and financed-emissions management in a setting where emissions are concentrated among a small number of firms.

title: Complex Systems as Structured Forgetting From Poisson-Liouville Mechanics to Emergent Meaning
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Complex Systems as Structured Forgetting From Poisson-Liouville Mechanics to Emergent Meaning
detail.abstract: This paper advances a unifying thesis for complexity science: complex systems exist because information is forgotten in a structured manner. Beginning with the Poisson-Liouville formulation of classical mechanics, we show that a world endowed with perfect informational memory is dynamically complete yet incapable of irreversibility, emergence, or meaning. We trace the progressive introduction of forgetting through statistical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics, before arriving at modern complexity science. The essay situates 'More is Different' as the ontological pivot where reductionism remains valid but insufficient and reframes 'The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics' as a consequence of selective abstraction rather than miracle. Drawing on far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics and selforganised criticality, the paper argues that complexity is neither disorder nor optimisation but the disciplined erosion of microstate memory. The result is a rigorous yet accessible framework linking physics, information, and meaning.

title: Delegation to Humans and Algorithms in Financial Decision Making
affiliations: Radboud University Nijmegen - Department of Economics, Radboud University Nijmegen - Department of Economics, University of Cambridge - Judge Business School and Radboud University, Institute for Management Research

detail.title: Delegation to Humans and Algorithms in Financial Decision Making
detail.abstract: We study how delegating financial decisions to humans or to automated, algorithmic systems affects reciprocity in credit relationships. Using a modified trust game, we show that borrowers are less likely to repay when lending decisions are delegated rather than made directly by the lender. This reduction in reciprocity is larger when the decision is delegated to an automated algorithm than to a human agent, even when monetary incentives and observability are held constant. At the same time, lenders are more willing to delegate to algorithmic than to human agents. Borrowers explain lower repayment after delegation, especially to algorithmic agents, by a perceived lack of lender effort and involvement. Our findings show that automation in financial decision making can weaken reciprocity and increase default risk by changing how borrowers perceive lender intentions.

title: Greenwashing in Sustainability Disclosures: A Systematic Review of Manifestations, Measurement, and Corporate Finance Implications
affiliations: University of York, University of York and University of York - The York Management School

detail.title: Greenwashing in Sustainability Disclosures: A Systematic Review of Manifestations, Measurement, and Corporate Finance Implications
detail.abstract: The evolution of sustainability reporting frameworks reflects a gradual shift from traditional financial and management accounting toward hybrid accounting frameworks intended to enhance organisations' transparency and accountability in environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities. Alongside these developments, concerns have emerged regarding ESG/CSR washing-commonly referred to as greenwashing-where firms mislead stakeholders through inflated, selective, or symbolic ESG disclosures. Despite a large and growing body of research, inconsistencies remain in both the conceptualisation and measurement of greenwashing, as well as in the interpretation of its implications for accounting and finance. In response, this study systematically reviews the greenwashing literature within the sustainability disclosure framework and shows that greenwashing manifests through disclosure manipulation, decoupling between symbol and substance in ESG reporting, strategic disclosure, and strategic partnerships, identifying fourteen unique manifestations. We examine how these typologies are operationalised in prior research using either direct firm-level measures or inferred relationships across variables. We then evaluate the decision usefulness of the identified direct measures and their implications for corporate finance research. Finally, we outline directions for future research to clarify the continuum, intent, extent, and thresholds of greenwashing, and highlight the corporate finance themes for which evidence remains limited.

title: Time as a Moral Lens
affiliations: WZB Berlin Social Science Center and New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi

detail.title: Time as a Moral Lens
detail.abstract: When do the costs of morally flawed decisions occur, at the moment of choice or only when negative consequences unfold later? We study this question using an experiment and structural estimations that exploit the temporal separation between actions and outcomes. By examining discounting behavior, we identify whether moral costs are experienced at the time of decision-making or when consequences materialize. Our findings suggest that in morally salient contexts such as lying, individuals bear costs immediately at the time of decision-making, consistent with a deontological perspective. In more neutral contexts, costs are discounted and arise when consequences materialize, aligning with a consequentialist view.

title: The Formation of New Centres of Economic Power and Influence Within the Contemporary Global Order
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: The Formation of New Centres of Economic Power and Influence Within the Contemporary Global Order
detail.abstract: The study analyses the systemic evolution of international economic relations from a unipolar to a polycentric structure. It investigates the rising economic capacity of emerging power centres—notably China, India, and ASEAN—and assesses their role in reconfiguring global influence vis-à-vis established powers such as the United States and the European Union. The core objective is to delineate the underlying dynamics of this power shift through a quantitative examination of Gross Domestic Product based on purchasing power parity (GDP PPP). The analysis seeks to measure changes in economic weight and to evaluate the contributions of regional integration blocs and Global South nations to the emerging world order. Employing a comparative methodology, the research utilises data from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank spanning 1995–2030. The primary analytical tool is the calculation of shares in global GDP (PPP) for both national economies and supranational entities. A critical component of the methodology involves appraising the consolidated economic potential of integration associations, with consideration given to their degree of economic coherence and institutional alignment. Key findings indicate a decisive shift in economic weight: developing nations now account for 59.27% of global GDP (PPP), surpassing the share of developed economies (39.36%). China’s position is affirmed at 19.68%, while India demonstrates substantial growth to 8.53%. ASEAN’s increasing economic significance is also highlighted. Concurrently, the relative shares of the US, the EU, and Japan are in decline. The analysis further reveals a pronounced concentration of economic capacity within the Global South, centred on a limited number of leading economies. The evidence points to the consolidation of a polycentric global economic architecture, with China, the US, and the EU constituting its principal pillars. The sustained expansion of India and ASEAN is identified as a catalyst for further complexity in the international balance of power. The study concludes that, due to profound internal disparities in development levels, the Global South does not presently constitute a cohesive and unified pole of economic influence within this new system.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used as virtual fi-nancial advisors for private clients in Switzerland. Given the rapid development of arti-ficial intelligence (AI) and the widespread availability of LLM-based chatbots, the question arises as to whether private individuals can use these technologies for compre-hensive financial self-advice as a potential substitute for professional financial advice. Using a zero-shot prompting approach, current state-of-the-art LLMs were evaluated using real exam questions at the Swiss tertiary education level. The evaluation was car-ried out both using an LLM-as-a-judge framework and by human experts. Overall, the results show that the models perform well. Many LLMs would pass a typical exam. At the same time, there are significant differences in performance between the models, subject areas and difficulty levels. Simple and conceptual questions are generally an-swered well, while performance declines significantly when it comes to more complex questions. Weaknesses are evident in questions relating to the consulting process and ethics, which require qualitative assessments and the integration of different perspec-tives. Despite the predominantly plausible answers, errors cannot be ruled out. Even the most powerful models fail to answer around a quarter of the questions correctly. In fi-nancial advice, this can have serious consequences. Overall, LLMs are not yet a suitable alternative to professional, holistic financial advice, but they can be used as a supporting tool with considerable potential. They are not yet suitable for non-professionals to use independently to create comprehensive financial plans.

detail.title: Free Rider Problem in Mixed Healthcare Systems: Behavioral Drivers, Overuse Patterns, and Implications for Benefit Design in Public Hospitals in Jordan
detail.abstract: Background: In Jordan, a middle-income country with a mixed healthcare system, persistent emergency department (ED) congestion raises questions about behavioral and institutional drivers beyond conventional supply–demand explanations. ED overuse represents a critical challenge for health system planning and cost containment.         Objective: This study examines ED overuse through a behavioral health economics lens, reframing non-urgent utilization as a system-level free-rider problem, and estimates its economic burden.         Methods: Using secondary data and national estimates, the study develops two indicators: an Emergency Department Overuse Index (EDOI) and a Free-Rider Proxy (FRP). Sensitivity analysis tests estimate robustness. Behavioral drivers—present bias, optimism bias, and loss aversion—are integrated with structural factors including limited primary care access and insurance design.         Results: Findings suggest substantial non-urgent ED utilization, generating an estimated financial burden of approximately 151.5 million JOD over five years. Sensitivity analysis confirms result stability. The interaction between behavioral incentives and system design amplifies inefficient service use in public hospitals.         Policy Implications: Results highlight the need for interventions beyond capacity expansion. Value-based insurance design, strengthened primary care gatekeeping, and behavioral nudges are proposed to align patient behavior with system efficiency while preserving equity.         Conclusion: By linking behavioral drivers with health system structure, this study provides a framework for addressing ED overuse in mixed healthcare systems, offering actionable insights for policymakers in middle-income countries.

title: Explainable Admission-Level Predictive Modeling for Prolonged Hospital Stay in Elderly Populations: Challenges in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
affiliations: Universidad de Antioquia, affiliation not provided to SSRN, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, Universidad de Antioquia, University of Antioquia and Universidad de Antioquia

detail.title: Explainable Admission-Level Predictive Modeling for Prolonged Hospital Stay in Elderly Populations: Challenges in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
detail.abstract: Prolonged length of stay (pLoS) is a significant factor associated with the risk of adverse in-hospital events. We develop and explain a predictive model  for pLos using admission-level patient and hospital administrative data. The approach includes a feature selection method by selecting non-correlated features with the highest information value. The method uses features weights of evidence to select a representative within cliques from graph theory. The prognosis study analyzed the records from 120,354 hospital admissions at the Hospital Alma Mater de Antioquia between January 2017 and March 2022. After a cleaning process the dataset was split into training (67\%), test (22\%), and validation (11\%) cohorts. A logistic regression model was trained to predict the pLoS in two classes: less than or greater than 7 days. The performance of the model was evaluated using accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC metrics. The feature selection method returns nine interpretable variables, enhancing the models' transparency. In the validation cohort, the pLoS model achieved a specificity of 0.83 (95\% CI, 0.82-0.84), sensitivity of 0.64 (95\% CI, 0.62-0.65), accuracy of 0.76 (95\% CI, 0.76-0.77), precision of 0.67 (95\% CI, 0.66-0.69), and AUC-ROC of 0.82 (95\% CI, 0.81-0.83). The model exhibits strong predictive performance and offers insights into the factors that influence prolonged hospital stays. This makes it a valuable tool for hospital management and for developing future intervention studies aimed at reducing pLoS.

title: Latent Changes in the Labor Share
affiliations: Utrecht University - School of Economics and Independent

detail.title: Latent Changes in the Labor Share
detail.abstract: Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019)'s canonical model of automation unambiguously predicts a decline in the labor share within sectors. Decomposing changes in the US labor share into within-sector and between-sector components, they show that within-sector changes indeed account for the bulk of the recent decline in the US labor share, while overall between-sector changes are quantitatively unimportant. However, by extending their single-sector framework to a multi-sector model and rooting it in an empirically tractable decomposition, this paper shows that the small overall between-sector component conceals substantial, though offsetting, equilibrium changes in consumer demand resulting from sector-specific changes in factor quantities and TFP growth. Although these equilibrium forces have not impacted overall between-sector changes in the US labor share so far, their importance indicates that ever-declining labor shares due to technological progress, such as AI, are not inevitable in the future.

title: Bridging the Tax Gap: A Proposal for Digital Access Fees in Cross-Border Cloud Transactions
affiliations: Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology

detail.title: Bridging the Tax Gap: A Proposal for Digital Access Fees in Cross-Border Cloud Transactions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study was influenced by my experience at Janssen Sanghavi & Associates, the teachings imparted to me by Dr. Dhruv Janssen Sanghavi, and my particular interest in international tax.

keywords: Article 12B of the UN Model Tax Convention

detail.abstract: The digital economy has outgrown the traditional concepts that have long underpinned international tax rules. Perhaps the most critical aspect with respect to cloud access transactions is determining the character of income resulting from such transactions. The character of income earned by a taxpayer directly impacts how such income is sourced and taxed under the laws of many countries. Due to the often-cross border nature of cloud computing services, both cloud services customers and providers are in of guidance on the proper characterization of payments arising from cloud service tax purposes. Capital-importing countries tend to have a broader concept of royalties because this allows them to expand their taxing rights, but capital-exporting countries tend to follow a more restrictive approach because they prefer to provide exclusive taxation rights to the country of residence. The lack of uniformity threatens to create further fragmentation and uncertainty in the international tax system. Should income derived from contracts within the realm of the cloud access payments constitute royalties, or services income? In response to this growing challenge, this paper proposes the creation of a new treaty category called "digital access fees". This new framework would offer a standardized approach to taxing cloud transactions, supported by a clear withholding tax mechanism.

title: COMPLEXITY: A Generalized Approach in Stata for Specialization Complexity Indices

detail.title: COMPLEXITY: A Generalized Approach in Stata for Specialization Complexity Indices
detail.abstract: We introduce complexity, a Stata command available on SSC that computes generalized complexity indices for specialization matrices. Originally developed for assessing economic complexity with global trade data (Hidalgo and Hausmann 2009), these metrics have since been extended to various domains including regional development, innovation, and labor economics. The complexity command implements three core methodologies: the eigenvector method (Hausmann et al. 2011a), the Method of Reflection (Hidalgo and Hausmann 2009), and the fitnesscomplexity approach (Tacchella et al. 2012). It also computes relatedness metrics such as coherence, adjacency matrices of the activity space network, and the complexity outlook as a measure of complexity potential. We describe the syntax and options, review the underlying algorithms, and provide applied examples.

title: Intermediary Asset Pricing with Passive Funds
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, University of Tübingen and Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Intermediary Asset Pricing with Passive Funds
detail.abstract: Passive investing has become an important component of financial markets. The passive fund industry in the United States has grown faster than the S&P 500 index, and more than one third of US equities are now owned by passive funds. We analyze the pricing implications of delegated passive investing within a stylized intermediary asset-pricing framework. First, we document that the compensation structure of passive funds exhibits non-monotonic features. In particular, institutional investors penalize not only underperformance but also outperformance relative to benchmarks, inducing funds to avoid deviations in both directions. Second, we study a stylized intermediary asset-pricing model in which the intermediary faces a quadratic penalty term in its incentive structure. We derive a closed-form solution for a passive fund's optimal deviation from its benchmark. We further show that the equity premium depends on (i) investor type and (ii) the extent of market frictions present in the economy. The equity premium is only mildly affected by passive funds owned by institutional investors. By contrast, it is strongly affected by active funds and by passive funds owned by retail investors. In these cases, we find pronounced intermediary asset-pricing effects on the equity premium.

title: Learning Through Simulation: Counselor Trainees' Interactions with ChatGPT as a Client

detail.title: Learning Through Simulation: Counselor Trainees' Interactions with ChatGPT as a Client
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored in counselor education, yet its pedagogical implications remain underexamined. This study investigated counselor trainees' experiences using ChatGPT (GPT-4o) as a simulated client for role-play practice, aiming to assess its potential benefits and limitations as a supplemental training tool. Using qualitative content analysis, AI-simulated counseling session transcripts were coded based on dimensions such as authenticity, emotional expression, consistency, self-awareness, and cultural dynamics. Additionally, a focus group interview provided insights into trainees' perceptions. Findings indicate that AI simulations offered a psychologically safe, flexible environment for practicing counseling skills, reducing performance anxiety, and fostering confidence before working with real clients. Participants emphasized the importance of detailed prompts to enhance realism and complexity, while noting limitations such as overly agreeable responses, lack of emotional nuance, and cultural neutrality unless explicitly prompted. Overall, trainees viewed AI as a valuable supplement rather than a replacement for live practice. These results suggest that generative AI can enhance experiential learning when integrated thoughtfully with structured guidance, ethical oversight, and culturally responsive design. Future research should explore strategies to improve authenticity and emotional depth in AI simulations to better support counselor competency development.

title: Calendar Anomalies: Real Patterns or Data-Mining Artifacts?
affiliations: University of Agder - School of Business and Law

detail.title: Calendar Anomalies: Real Patterns or Data-Mining Artifacts?
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines well-known calendar anomalies in equity returns with the objective of determining whether these effects are genuine return regularities or artifacts of data mining. We study four canonical anomaly families-the day-of-the-week, week-of-themonth, month-of-the-year (January), and Sell-in-May effects-using U.S. equity data, and we also evaluate international evidence for the Sell-in-May effect. Our methodology explicitly accounts for the selection inherent in the discovery of calendar anomalies by applying data-mining-adjusted bootstrap tests that mimic a researcher's within-family search across alternative calendar definitions. Our results show that, after correcting for data mining, the day-of-the-week, week-of-the-month, and month-of-the-year anomalies remain statistically significant in the full sample and, in particular, in the pre-1990 period, indicating that these effects were not merely statistical artifacts. At the same time, we confirm that these anomalies largely disappear in post-1990 data. In contrast, the Sell-in-May effect proves more resilient: international evidence remains robust to data-mining concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that several calendar anomalies were real features of historical return data, even though their economic relevance has diminished in more recent decades.

title: Introduction to Fairness in International Taxation
affiliations: University of Surrey - School of Law and Independent

detail.title: Introduction to Fairness in International Taxation
detail.abstract: This is the Introduction for Fairness in International Taxation, an edited volume published by Hart Publishing and edited by Ira K Lindsay and Benita Mathew (www.bloomsbury.com/uk/fairness-in-international-taxation-9781509968077/).  The book explores the thorny normative issues raised by the changing landscape of international tax policy.  Proposals for taxation of the digital economy and the OECD/G20 BEPS framework promise fundamental changes in the international tax system. The book features perspectives from legal scholars, political theorists, and political philosophers on international corporate and individual taxation. Contributors advance new theories of international tax justice, develop theoretically informed reform proposals and critique influential approaches to international tax reform. Key themes include justice in bilateral and multilateral international tax agreements, the taxation of cross-border workers, fair division of tax revenue from multinational corporations, and the fairness of the international tax policy-making process.  The book provides new perspectives on leading international tax policy debates, analyses the intersection between international distributive justice and contemporary tax policy, and proposes innovative ways to meet the demands of tax justice in a global context.

title: Sarees: Culture, Commerce, Constitutionalism
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Sarees: Culture, Commerce, Constitutionalism
detail.abstract: This article explores how sarees, as cultural artefacts, have been failed by conventional intellectual property laws which understand authorship and ownership through Western individualistic paradigms rather than through paths of communal continuity. Weaving together mythology, commercial constraints, and technological implications, it suggests that sarees may be better protected by turning more strongly towards India's own Constitution and its understanding of the public interest.

title: Prediction Markets 2.0 (English Version)
affiliations: Luiss - Guido Carli (Dpt. of Economics and Finance) and Guglielmo Marconi University

detail.title: Prediction Markets 2.0 (English Version)
detail.abstract: In recent years, prediction markets have experienced rapid growth, returning to the center of the economic and financial debate as tools for aggregating information about future events. This paper analyzes the recent evolution of prediction markets, placing them within the broader context of derivatives markets and highlighting the informational content and signaling power of prices. After discussing the relationship between exchange-traded and over-the-counter markets, the paper examines several emblematic cases-including contracts on the capture of Abu Musab al-Zarqawi and the removal of Nicolás Maduro-that illustrate how prediction market prices can incorporate relevant information very quickly, often ahead of its full dissemination through traditional information channels. The paper also compares the forecasting performance of prediction markets with that of opinion polls and selected structural models used to predict electoral outcomes. Finally, key regulatory issues are discussed, including insider trading and cryptocurrencies. The value of prediction markets lies less in the ex post accuracy of individual forecasts than in their ability to make uncertainty about complex events observable and measurable, thereby providing a useful informational complement to public and private decision-making.

title: The Application of Sen's Capability Approach in Disability Research: A Critical Interpretive Synthesis.
affiliations: University of Agder, KU Leuven - Faculty of Business and Economics (FEB) and University of Agder

detail.title: The Application of Sen's Capability Approach in Disability Research: A Critical Interpretive Synthesis.
detail.abstract: The use of Sen's Capability Approach (CA) in disability research has become increasingly popular, and this paper reviews how CA has been used to inform empirical disability research. We conducted a critical interpretive synthesis of 43 articles identified from Web of Science and Scopus databases. Our findings unveil the multifaceted role of Capability Approach (CA) as both a foundational framework for disability research, and an outcome measurement tool, enabling researchers to assess capabilities, well-being, and functionings. Our review accomplishes more than just demonstrating the versatility of CA in various disability research designs but also makes a significant contribution to the field by proposing a novel future research framework grounded in the CA perspective. This framework offers valuable guidance for researchers aiming to advance disability scholarship through a capabilitarian lens. By building on the strengths CA identified in this review, future research can leverage CA to create a more inclusive and holistic approach to disability.

title: The Extractive Co-Option Mechanism: Envy, Narrative, and the Persistence of Inequality from Covenant to Code

detail.title: The Extractive Co-Option Mechanism: Envy, Narrative, and the Persistence of Inequality from Covenant to Code

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Extractive Co-Option Mechanism (ECM) as a unified theoretical framework for understanding the remarkable persistence of extractive institutional logic across five millennia of monetary and political history. Rather than treating persistence as institutional failure or static path dependence, the ECM models it as a dynamic, adaptive process driven by elites' strategic management of mass envy through narrative mobilization, boundary reconstruction, and institutional reproduction. We formalize this process using social-comparison microfoundations, continuous-time dynamics, and an optimal-stopping boundary for elimination equilibria. Empirical diagnostics on U.S. data (1971-2024) illustrate how the mechanism's components-Envy Gradient, Narrative Buffer, and Elite Fragmentation-operate in a modern context and identify periods of heightened instability without requiring precise prediction of reset timing.

title: A Review on Global Trends and Challenges in Papaya Production

detail.title: A Review on Global Trends and Challenges in Papaya Production
detail.abstract: Papaya is a very perishable fruit, and challenges such as postharvest losses, diseases, and environmental factors influence its production worldwide. Hence, postharvest management is the major concern in maintaining quality and prolonging the shelf life. This review synthesizes studies that analyze effective postharvest treatments, disease management, and improved farming methods to enhance the quality and yield of Papaya. Ten (10) published research studies from 2013-2023 were reviewed from multiple sources to identify and evaluate the worldwide status of the papaya industry. Most of the research studies came from India, Malaysia, Mexico, China, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and a few from the Philippines. Important approaches involve incorporating established and innovative cultural management methods such as integrated nutrient management involving the application of bio-fertilizers and biocontrol agents to improve nutrient absorption and disease resistance, precision farming practices, enhanced postharvest management, which comprises physical treatments, hot water treatment, irradiation, ozonation, and low-temperature methods and natural methods, particularly essential oils, chitosan, and microbes in preserving fruit quality. In addition, genetic technology, which consists of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, showed possibilities for generating PRSV-resistant transgenic papaya varieties to improve papaya durability. The results demonstrate the various approaches for better productivity. Further research studies and modifications are necessary for long-term sustainability and profitable papaya production.

title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) A Unified Optimal Control Framework for the Stable Lifetime of Capitalism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) A Unified Optimal Control Framework for the Stable Lifetime of Capitalism
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM), a unified optimal-control framework that endogenously determines the remaining stable lifetime of capitalism as an outcome of debt accumulation. Capitalism operates only under the natural inequality: R > g > i > 0 where R denotes the return on capital, g the economic growth rate, and i the policy interest rate. We introduce policy freedom α(D), a decreasing function of total debt D, which constrains the feasible range of monetary policy. As debt accumulates, policy freedom erodes endogenously, eventually preventing the maintenance of g > i and triggering structural collapse̶without reliance on exogenous shocks, political failures, or market irrationality. Using Bellman dynamic programming and Hamiltonian optimal control, we derive the optimal interest-rate path i*(t) that maximizes the duration of R > g > i > 0. DICM integrates macro-level natural laws, meso-level firm investment incentives, and micro-level household carry behavior into a single dynamic system. This paper presents the first framework to quantify capitalismʼs finite stable lifespan as a structurally determined outcome of debt dynamics.

title: Predictive Analytics for Financial Distress: A Machine Learning Approach to Bankruptcy Prediction

detail.title: Predictive Analytics for Financial Distress: A Machine Learning Approach to Bankruptcy Prediction

keywords: Predictive Analytics for Financial Distress: A Machine Learning Approach to Bankruptcy Prediction

detail.abstract:
A key element of financial risk management that affects investors, auditors, and regulatory agencies is the prediction of financial distress and bankruptcy. Despite being widely used for decades, traditional models like Zmijewski's Probit Model and Altman's Z-Score have limitations in complex and dynamic financial environments. To improve financial distress prediction, this study investigates the use of machine learning techniques, specifically Random Forests, Decision Trees, and Logistic Regression. The study selects features using Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) on the Bankruptcy Prediction Dataset from Kaggle and evaluates model performance using important metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.

According to the results, the Random Forest model performed better than traditional methods, with an AUC-ROC score of 0.90 and 97% accuracy, making it the most reliable predictive model. Despite having a slightly lower accuracy rate of 95%, the Decision Tree model showed excellent interpretability, which made it perfect for stakeholder engagement. Despite having a high AUC-ROC score (0.93), logistic regression had poor recall, which limited its application. All machine learning models showed significant improvements in predictive accuracy and overall effectiveness when compared to Altman's Z-Score, which achieved 70% accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.65.

Despite machine learning models' superior performance, issues like class imbalance and the requirement for more interpretabilities still exist. To improve predictive accuracy and functionality, suggestions include real-time implementation, industry-specific model customization, and the incorporation of non-financial indicators. The potential of machine learning-driven financial distress prediction as a potent risk management tool that facilitates more proactive financial decision-making and reduces the financial impact of business failures is highlighted in this study.

title: Modeling the Effect of Social Contagion in Solar Adoption through Commuter and Socioeconomic Networks

detail.title: Modeling the Effect of Social Contagion in Solar Adoption through Commuter and Socioeconomic Networks
detail.abstract: The widespread adoption of residential solar panels is critical for the global energy transition, but its progress is hindered by challenges such as high customer acquisition costs and slowing demand. While social contagion is known to be a powerful driver of increasing solar adoption, the exact mechanisms within this "peer effect" remain poorly distinguished. Specifically, a gap exists in understanding whether influence spreads primarily through Information Flow-that is, through interaction and connections-or through Socioeconomic Similarity (homophily), where influence is stronger within groups of more similar socioeconomic characteristics, such as income, race, and education levels. This study aims to quantitatively distinguish between these two competing mechanisms for solar adoption, hypothesizing that if the principle of homophily – as opposed to information flow-was the dominant mechanism in social contagion for solar adoption, then a network model built on socioeconomic similarity would produce communities with more uniform solar adoption rates and correlate more strongly with real-world adoption data. To test this, network science was used to create three networks that allowed for comparison. Each of these networks were created at a U.S. county level: a Socioeconomic Similarity Network connecting geographically proximate counties based on a multi-dimensional similarity score from demographic and economic profiles; an Information Flow Network built from county-to-county commuter flows; and a State-Level Network to provide a geographic baseline for comparison. Then, a static analysis was conducted using the Louvain algorithm to identify community structures and measure their homogeneity, and then used a Susceptible-Infected-Resistant (SIR) epidemiological model to test which network structure's diffusion patterns best correlate with the real-world solar adoption data. It was found that while the Socioeconomic Network was effective at identifying homogeneous clusters of existing adopters through the Louvain algorithm, the Commuter Network was the only model whose dynamic diffusion patterns produced a strong and statistically significant positive correlation with actual county-level adoption rates. Our results suggest two combined models of social contagion, where real-world interaction pathways (proxied by commuter ties) act as the primary channels for influence, while socioeconomic similarity models the local receptiveness to that influence. These findings demonstrate that effective solar adoption policies must leverage both broad information channels and targeted, peer-based community engagement, rather than relying on a single mechanism. A successful campaign to increase solar adoption should recognize the pathways that operate in the diffusion of their message and use socioeconomic characteristics to increase receptivity.

title: A Sharia-Compliant, Heterogeneous-Agent, Asset Pricing Model: With Asset Allocation and Risk-Adjusted Performance
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: A Sharia-Compliant, Heterogeneous-Agent, Asset Pricing Model: With Asset Allocation and Risk-Adjusted Performance
detail.abstract:
The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), is the basis of finance theory and practice globally. Having been developed in the Anglo-Saxon world, it excludes an entire population of followers of Islamic Finance. As of 2020, Muslims made up over 25% of the world population, and Hindus nearly 15%. The attempts to modify CAPM to sharia principles have typically been to either exclude the traditional risk-free rate (as it is not sharia- compliant) via the use of the Zero Beta CAPM, and/or modify the “market portfolio” (by picking a sharia-compliant “risky” portfolio). Sharia-compliance requires (i) no interest charges, as Islamic economics prohibits the active practice of the levy interest called usury (riba); (ii) imposition of zakat for income - Zakat is an obligation payment to pay net assets as well as a form of distributing wealth from people who have excess assets to those in need.

Prof. Cochrane has suggested that, “Switching to a payoff perspective may change lots of procedures in finance”, and two new (heterogeneous) financial innovations in Brazil for ensuring retirement security (RendA+) and a child’s education (Educa+), deemed sharia- compliant by a Turkish Islamic scholar, open the way to a Islamic Finance centric, Sharia- compliant Heterogeneous-agent Asset Pricing Model (SCHAPM), with useful implications for portfolio structure (asset allocation) and risk-return examination (risk-adjusted performance). SCHAPM uses observable sharia-compliant assets and risk preferences parameters, eliminates "free parameters", and lends itself to a general equilibrium model of assets and wages too. It offers a new pathway to a realistic, broader SCHAPM as assets not sharia-compliant can be priced in this model, unlike the models of traditional finance, which lack such flexibility. Simply put, it is a Copernican revolution of finance, or maybe more appropriately Al-Khwarizmian, as all we need is basic algebra to develop SCHAPM.
