title: Bank Macroprudential Policies and Borrower ESG Performance
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management - Accounting Department, Newcastle University, University of Zurich - Department Finance and University of Queensland

detail.title: Bank Macroprudential Policies and Borrower ESG Performance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 26-13
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the cross-border transmission of macroprudential policies to corporate ESG performance. Constructing a novel measure of U.S. firms' exposure to foreign regulatory shocks through syndicated lending relationships, we employ a triple-difference design that exploits variation across countries, banks, and time. We document significant and economically meaningful spillovers: U.S. borrowers exposed to foreign banks subject to capital or liquidity tightening experience significant declines in ESG performance, whereas exposure to loosening measures leads to ESG improvements. These effects are primarily driven by environmental and governance dimensions. We establish causality using the 2014 European Asset Quality Review as an exogenous regulatory shock, complemented by evidence from the staggered adoption of Basel III and stacked event-study analyses. Overall, our findings highlight an important real consequence of international bank regulation, showing that macroprudential policies can shape corporate sustainability outcomes through global credit markets.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Custom and Pre-trained CNN Models for Image Classification on Bangladeshi Real-World Datasets
affiliations: University of Dhaka, University of Dhaka and University of Dhaka

detail.title: Comparative Evaluation of Custom and Pre-trained CNN Models for Image Classification on Bangladeshi Real-World Datasets
detail.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely used for image classification, yet their performance strongly depends on dataset complexity and deployment constraints. This study presents a comparative evaluation of custom-designed CNN architectures and popular pre-trained models on five real-world image datasets from Bangladesh, spanning agricultural and infrastructural applications. The tasks include mango variety classification (15 classes), paddy disease classification (35 classes), and three binary classification problems: road damage, footpath encroachment, and auto-rickshaw detection. In addition to task-specific CNNs, VGG16 and ResNet50 are evaluated using fixed feature extraction and transfer learning strategies. The results show that transfer learning, particularly with ResNet50, achieves the highest accuracy on complex multi-class datasets, while custom CNNs deliver competitive performance on binary tasks with substantially lower computational cost. These findings emphasize the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency and highlight the importance of selecting model architectures based on dataset characteristics and deployment requirements.

title: Automation in Tax Filing: Benefits and Risks

detail.title: Automation in Tax Filing: Benefits and Risks
detail.abstract: The automation of tax filing processes has emerged as a critical innovation in modern accounting and public finance. By leveraging digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and automated data processing tools, tax filing automation promises to enhance efficiency, accuracy, and compliance while reducing administrative burdens for both taxpayers and authorities (Smith 2022). This study examines the current state of tax filing automation through a systematic review of academic literature, analysis of case studies from leading accounting firms and government agencies, and evaluation of statistical data on adoption rates and performance outcomes (Johnson and Lee 2023). Key findings indicate that automated tax systems improve operational efficiency by reducing manual data entry, minimizing errors through algorithmic validation, and facilitating timely compliance with filing deadlines (Brown 2021). Furthermore, automation supports better auditability and real-time monitoring of taxpayer submissions, enhancing transparency and accountability (Martinez et al. 2022). However, the adoption of automated tax systems also presents risks, including potential breaches of sensitive financial data, ethical concerns regarding algorithmic bias, and errors resulting from system misconfigurations (Williams 2023). The study concludes that while tax filing automation offers substantial benefits for taxpayers, accounting firms, and policymakers, careful implementation, robust cybersecurity measures, and continuous monitoring are essential to mitigate associated risks. Policymakers are encouraged to establish clear regulatory frameworks and ethical guidelines, while firms should invest in employee training and system oversight. Overall, automation represents a transformative step toward more efficient, accurate, and transparent tax administration (Smith 2022).

title: A rotated Dynamic Factor Model for the Yield Curve: Squeezing out Information when it Matters
affiliations: Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM) and Polytechnic University of Marche

detail.title: A rotated Dynamic Factor Model for the Yield Curve: Squeezing out Information when it Matters
detail.abstract: The yield curve is widely regarded as a powerful descriptor of the economy and market expectations. A common approach to its statistical representation relies on a small number of factors summarizing the curve, which can then be used to forecast real economic activity. We argue that optimal factor extraction is crucial for retrieving information when considering an approximate factor model. By introducing a rotation of the model including cointegration, we reduce cross-sectional dependence in the idiosyncratic components. This leads to improved forecasts of key macroeconomic variables during periods of economic and financial instability, both in the US and the euro area.

title: Evaluating Policy Compliance and Enforcement in Urban Land Use Planning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating Policy Compliance and Enforcement in Urban Land Use Planning
detail.abstract: Urban land use planning plays a critical role in shaping sustainable urban forms, with policy compliance and enforcement serving as central mechanisms to ensure orderly development (Mwangi, 2024; Thompson & George-Ibikiri, 2024). Despite the existence of comprehensive urban planning frameworks, uneven adherence to regulations and weak enforcement practices often undermine sustainable growth objectives. This study aims to assess compliance levels, evaluate enforcement effectiveness, and identify challenges in the implementation of urban planning policies across selected case studies. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research integrates GIS mapping, policy analysis, field surveys, and statistical evaluation to provide a holistic understanding of urban land use governance (Ahsan et al., 2023; Riungu & Kathuri, 2024). Findings reveal significant disparities in compliance across different urban zones, highlight limitations in monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, and underscore the influence of governance gaps on policy effectiveness (Mottelson, 2023; Zeng et al., 2023). The study also demonstrates the interplay between administrative capacity, stakeholder engagement, and regulatory oversight in shaping urban development outcomes. The main conclusion emphasizes that achieving sustainable urban growth requires stronger regulatory frameworks, targeted capacity-building initiatives, and integrated monitoring systems to enhance compliance and enforce planning policies effectively. These insights provide actionable guidance for policymakers, urban planners, and local authorities seeking to foster sustainable, well-regulated urban environments.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming military capabilities, from predictive targeting to autonomous command systems. While the United States and China dominate the AI arms race through scale, the European Union (EU) emphasizes regulation and ethics. Thus, the EU lacks a unified defense AI doctrine, with innovation fragmented across member states and reliance on dual-use civilian R&D. Existing literature often addresses AI ethics or greatpower competition but gives less attention to Europe's vulnerabilities in defense AI. This paper conducts a comparative analysis of defense AI ecosystems in the United States (US), China, Russia, Israel, and the European Union, examining investment models, innovation frameworks, and regulation. An analytical lens of regulatory capacity versus strategic capability is applied to highlight tradeoffs. The analysis shows that the US defense AI strategy is driven by private sector partnerships, China by state-led integration, and Israel by military innovation, while the EU's cautious framework hinders defense application. Furthermore, the EU risks becoming a consumer rather than a producer of sovereign technologies. To address this gap, the paper proposes adapting the Global Partnership on AI's (GPAI) Security and Safety infrastructure for the European defense-AI sector, alongside EU-level mechanisms to enforce accountability and ethical safeguards while expanding capacity.

detail.abstract: The 2008 and 2020 financial crises share a common feature: both erupted during periods of historically low volatility. This paper tests whether principles from Resilience Engineering operate in financial markets. A novel measure, Accumulated Spectral Fragility (ASF), operationalizes the concept of "absorptive capacity" by capturing the persistence of low-dimensional correlation structures. The empirical analysis confirms five theoretical predictions: (P1) elevated expectations suppress signal processing (β =-0.034, p = 0.004); (P2) signal suppression increases coordination (β =-0.045, p = 0.002); (P3) coordination amplifies tail risk conditionally (β = 0.071, p = 0.003); (P4) career risk heterogeneity predicts institutional differences (p < 0.001); and (P5) regulatory changes produce predicted coordination effects in four natural experiments. The 2000-2007 period provides critical validation: ASF remained elevated without crisis because funding constraints did not bind, demonstrating that coordination is necessary but not sufficient for systemic failure. The three-way interaction of coordination, expectations, and stress (β 7 = 8.945, t = 3.67) captures maximum amplification when all conditions align. These findings reconcile the volatility paradox and suggest that stability creates fragility through coordination that eliminates absorptive capacity.

detail.title: Organization Capital, Bond Issuance Spread, and Debt Financing Choices
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between firm-level organization capital and corporate bond issuance spreads. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in firm-level organization capital is associated with a 11.74% increase in corporate bond issuance yield spreads, consistent with organization capital elevating risk. The effect remains robust after addressing endogeneity and is stronger for firms with a higher risk of key talent leaving. We further find that firms with higher organization capital rely more on bank loans than on public bonds, likely because bank financing is cheaper. Moreover, they choose shorter debt maturities, issue more short-term debt, and maintain higher leverage. The evidence highlights the central role of organization capital in shaping firms’ cost of issuing public debt and financing choices.

detail.title: Evaluating Green Infrastructure Interventions for Urban Flood Mitigation
detail.abstract: Urban flooding has emerged as a critical global challenge as climate change, accelerated urbanisation, land-use modification, and increasing pressure on drainage infrastructure intensify flood risks in cities worldwide (Khodadad et al.; Wang et al.). In response to these challenges, this study conducts a comparative evaluation of green infrastructure (GI) interventions for urban flood mitigation using GIS-based flood susceptibility analysis, systematic literature synthesis, and empirical evidence from selected urban case studies, including spatial assessments of flood-prone areas in Lagos (Urban Flood Susceptibility in Lagos; Li et al.). The methodological framework integrates spatial modelling with policy-oriented analysis to assess how GI performs across different urban contexts and governance environments (Khodadad et al.; Wang et al.). Findings indicate that GI interventions significantly reduce surface runoff, enhance infiltration capacity, and improve stormwater retention while complementing conventional grey infrastructure systems (Herath et al.; Esraz-Ul-Zannat et al.). However, the effectiveness of GI varies considerably depending on spatial scale, land-use configuration, institutional capacity, and planning enforcement mechanisms (Li et al.; Urban Flood Susceptibility in Lagos). The study concludes that green infrastructure represents a viable and sustainable urban flood mitigation strategy when strategically integrated into spatial planning frameworks, supported by GIS-based decision-support systems, and aligned with long-term climate adaptation policies (Khodadad et al.; Wang et al.).

title: Transfer Pricing Compliance among Multinational Corporations in Developing Economies

detail.title: Transfer Pricing Compliance among Multinational Corporations in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Transfer pricing today is front and center for tax authorities in many developing countries and for good reason. It touches revenue collection, fairness in the tax system, and how governments regulate big multinational firms. As cross-border deals and intra-group transactions grow, gaps in transfer pricing compliance leave poorer countries particularly vulnerable to base erosion and profit shifting. This paper pulls together empirical studies, legal analyses, and policy work on the topic, with a clear bent toward issues faced by developing economies. What comes through, again and again, are persistent weaknesses: shaky enforcement, clever regulatory arbitrage by multinationals, a big information gap between taxpayers and tax authorities, and simply not enough administrative or technical muscle within revenue agencies. The review also flags a common problem: the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines are a useful global touchstone, sure, but they don't work like magic when you just copy them in without fitting them to local laws, institutions, and economic realities. The main takeaway? Leaning only on international standards won't fix these compliance problems. Instead, the study argues for a blended approach that includes regulatory reform plus beefed-up audit and admin capacity, clearer transparency tools, and stronger international cooperation for sharing information and providing technical help (Kalra and Afzal; Eukeria and Mpofu; Mashiri et al.; Pareno).

title: Evaluating Public Awareness Campaigns for Improving Disaster Preparedness

detail.title: Evaluating Public Awareness Campaigns for Improving Disaster Preparedness
detail.abstract:
This report assesses the impact of public awareness campaigns on different communities' preparedness for disasters. The goal of this research study was to understand whether the campaigns improved the public's awareness and to what extent they changed their behaviors and increased the resiliency of their communities. The study used a combination of methods: an analysis of the survey conducted with 1200 people from 3 regions, an analysis of the Geographical Information Systems (GIS) for drawing awareness to the risk and the accessibility of the resources, and an analysis of the existing educational programs. The surveys indicated that there was a lack of understanding about the available emergency procedures and that this lack of understanding was prevalent in the rural and more dangerous areas. The communications methods used (i.e., social media, community workshops, and local radio) were effective in different ways in different communities and with different demographics.
The GIS mapping analysis indicated that there were a number of areas that had low participation, which justified the need for an activity to improve participation in these areas. The analysis of educational programs indicated that in the more active, participatory workshops, people were able to better retain the information about safety procedures than in the more passive ones. The most significant finding from the analysis was that general preparedness campaigns created awareness. However, there was a need for more focus on more specific preparedness campaigns to achieve a higher level of awareness and preparedness behaviors. The report indicated that the combination of new technologies with community invitations yields the best results. Policymakers and emergency management agencies should be encouraged to use and implement a specific approach to the region and use data-driven methodology to help with the optimization of resource distribution and the engagement of the public. Future projects should implement some form of iterative evaluation based on real-time assessments and should establish and maintain collaborations with local government officials, schools, and community groups to sustain preparedness.

detail.title: Digital Invisibility and Revenue Loss in Small Construction Firms: A Market Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the relationship between contractor credentials (measured by BuildZoom scores) and search visibility in digital markets. Using a sample of 20 Tampa Bay general contractors with annual revenues $1M-$10M, we find that superior technical credentials (BuildZoom scores 110+, indicating top 2% performance) do not correlate with search engine rankings for high-intent customer queries. Contractors with exceptional credentials frequently remain invisible in search results while competitors with 15-20 point lower scores dominate page one rankings. We quantify the revenue impact of this visibility gap at $330,000-$500,000 annually per contractor. The analysis suggests that established small construction firms face systematic discovery constraints as consumer research behavior shifts to digital-first channels, with 78% of homeowners conducting online research before contractor contact. We propose a visibility optimization framework addressing credential presentation, review generation, and search positioning. The findings have implications for small business client acquisition strategy in industries where technical competence and digital discoverability operate as independent variables.

detail.abstract: The geography, infrastructure, and legacy 911 systems' structural inefficiencies (Newgard et al.) have caused ongoing delays in rural public emergency response systems to become even more critical public safety threats. As a result, interest in alternative systems, such as Next Generation 911 (NG911), capable of serving more underserved communities, has grown in rural emergency response systems. This research conducts a mixed-methods synthesis of rural empirical case studies, remote sensing (GIS) evaluations, and system-performance literature to investigate the outcomes of rural NG911 implementations (Richardson and Murphy; Horan et al.). Implementation evidence, spatial performance, and operational effectiveness documentation were primary data sources for this work. The evidence suggests NG911 implementations result in shorter average call-processing times and improved responder coordination and location accuracy with higher tiers of system integration. However, data suggest this is an ongoing issue that can and has improved public safety, and emergency response operational efficiencies if system integration is present, but at inconsistent and at times very low levels, across jurisdictions (Access to Emergency Care in Rural Illinois; Seeman et al.). The study concludes that NG911 can substantially improve rural emergency response effectiveness, but only when embedded within interoperable data ecosystems and supported by sustained training, governance reforms, and cross-agency coordination. Without these enabling conditions, technological upgrades alone are unlikely to resolve persistent rural response inequities (Goldstein; Designing and Evaluating Interactive Web Maps).

detail.abstract: This paper introduces AROHI (Advanced Road Optimization & Harvesting Intelligence), a novel interdisciplinary framework integrating energy harvesting, smart infrastructure, and AI-driven optimization into road networks. By embedding piezoelectric, electromagnetic, and solar harvesting units within highways and combining them with AI-driven traffic control and blockchain-based data validation, AROHI proposes a sustainable model for both renewable energy generation and intelligent transportation management. The proposed system not only provides additional energy for electric vehicles and smart grids but also addresses challenges of congestion, monitoring, and real-time optimization. The prototype successfully implemented blockchain validation with Markov Chain prediction, though energy generation and GPS tracking showed deviations requiring material optimization. title: Evaluating OECD Guidelines in Controlling Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)

detail.title: Evaluating OECD Guidelines in Controlling Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)
detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to determine how successful the recommendations issued by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) concerning Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) are in tackling profit shifting and tax base erosion by multinational companies. Though regime features have been adopted, the questions will continue to concern the levels of substantive compliance, particularly concerning differing country contexts. The study aims to provide a qualitative approach and blends a systematic review of the pertinent academic and policy literature with a comparative assessment of the implementation of the BEPS across selected jurisdictions. The findings show that, even though the implementation of this BEPS has resulted in the achievement of some levels of transparency, policy alignment, and awareness of the aggressive tax planning syndrome, the implementation of the BEPS is still partial and uneven. The implementation of the BEPS initiative has yielded results that are disparate between the developing and developed countries, because the developing countries have a more pronounced level of structural challenges, such as inadequate administrative capacity, information asymmetries, and poor enforcement, which mitigate the impact of the BEPS on profit shifting and the protection of the domestic tax base. The study emphasises that even though the OECD BEPS recommendations are not sufficient, they provide a good starting point to be built on. An appropriate conclusion can be outlined for the study in question. The OECD BEPS recommendations indeed offer the necessary foundation for global cooperation in taxation. However, from the perspective of global taxation cooperation, the results of global accounting taxation will still be weak. This can be attributed to the lack of the required contextual adaptation, development of implementation capacities, and additional enforcement in the weaker regions of the globe. In filling the gap of literature in taxation, international accounting taxation, and policies, the study emphasizes the relevance of the implementation gap, i.e., for the OECD and BEPS empirical studies, the so-called 'OECD-focused literature. ' Effectiveness in BEPS is a persistent gap in the literature.

title: The Impact of Digital Payment Adoption on Income Volatility in India's Informal Retail Sector

detail.title: The Impact of Digital Payment Adoption on Income Volatility in India's Informal Retail Sector
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether digital payment adoption reduces income volatility for small retail businesses in India. While existing studies largely focus on revenue growth, this research shifts attention toward income stability and risk, which are often more important for micro-enterprises operating under financial uncertainty. The study uses micro-level data from 25 small retailers, including kirana stores, tea stalls, mobile shops, and stationery stores, and compares monthly revenue patterns before and after digital payments became widely used. Income risk is measured using revenue volatility, the coefficient of variation, and the frequency of below-average income months. The analysis finds that higher digital payment usage is associated with lower income volatility, fewer bad months, and reduced payment delays. Shops with a high share of digital transactions show noticeably smoother income flows compared to low adopters, even when average revenue gains are modest. These findings suggest that digital payments contribute to financial resilience by improving cash flow predictability. The results matter for financial inclusion and MSME policy, as they highlight the role of digital payments not only in increasing transactions, but also in reducing income risk for small businesses in the informal sector.

detail.abstract: China's large-scale reforestation campaigns have long been promoted as a global environmental success narrative, contributing to climate mitigation, combating desertification, and restoring degraded ecosystems. However, recent scientific findings indicate that large-scale afforestation programs have also produced unexpected hydrological consequences, fundamentally altering national water distribution patterns. Between 2001 and 2020, increased evapotranspiration driven by expanded forest cover intensified atmospheric moisture recycling, redistributing water across regions and leading to declining net water availability in eastern and northwestern China, while the Tibetan Plateau experienced relative gains. These findings demonstrate that environmentally "virtuous" policies may generate systemic externalities when adopted without comprehensive hydrological and strategic environmental assessment. This paper examines the legal, regulatory, economic, and governance implications of China's experience, highlighting risks to water security, agricultural planning, and environmental policymaking. The discussion advances a broader reflection on precaution, strategic environmental assessment, and evidence-based climate governance-extracting lessons relevant not only to China, but to Brazil and other developing nations.

detail.abstract:
This preprint presents JOR Framework v3, a methodology for evaluating Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) using Bayesian posterior analysis. The framework combines the James Orion Report (JOR) system with probabilistic reasoning to provide structured, evidence-driven analysis.

It quantifies Solid Object Probability (SOP), the likelihood a physical event occurred, and Non-Human Probability (NHP), an anomaly-weighted score indicating deviation from conventional explanations. By integrating witness credibility, environmental conditions, and physical/sensor evidence, the framework produces weighted SOP and NHP scores. Bayesian updating calculates posterior probabilities, ensuring non-human hypotheses are evaluated on a solid evidentiary foundation.

Version 3 updates include formatting corrections, a Limitations and Future Work section, and a corrected human-likelihood formula. Two illustrative cases demonstrate practical application: Tier 1 UAP — Aguadilla, Puerto Rico (2013) and Tier 2 UAP — Socorro, New Mexico (1964).

JOR Framework v3 supports reproducible, transparent, and systematic analysis, enabling automated evaluation, rapid assessment of new cases, and integration with probabilistic programming tools for future research.

title: The Rise of the Gilded Zombie: Monetary Policy Transmission and Sectoral Vulnerability in the FTSE 350 (2020-2024)

detail.title: The Rise of the Gilded Zombie: Monetary Policy Transmission and Sectoral Vulnerability in the FTSE 350 (2020-2024)
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the evolution of corporate zombification within the UK's FTSE 350 index during the transition from a decade of ultra-low interest rates to the post-2022 inflationary environment. Utilizing a multi-stage filtering process based on Interest Coverage Ratios (ICR) and firm age, we identify a burgeoning class of "Gilded Zombies", large-cap, asset-heavy firms exhibiting persistent financial distress despite their systemic importance. Our analysis reveals a significant correlation between the Bank of England's rate hikes (from 0.1% to 5.25%) and a spike in zombie density, particularly within the Real Estate (29.0%) and Basic Materials (22.0%) sectors. Crucially, we find that zombie firms are significantly less productive than their healthy peers, generating only £0.44 of revenue per £1 of assets compared to £0.76 for non-zombies. By constructing a transition matrix for the 2022-2024 period, we categorize the distressed population into "Chronic Zombies" (40.7% of the distressed cohort), "New Victims" (34.6%), and "Lazarus" recoveries (59.2%). We conclude that while a segment of the FTSE 350 demonstrates resilience, a core group of "Chronic" firms remains trapped in structural distress, creating a capital congestion problem that exacerbates the UK's long-term productivity puzzle.

detail.title: Soft Budget Constraint and Growth through the Lens of a Schumpeterian Model
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of the soft budget constraint in shaping firm dynamics and long-run economic growth. We develop a Schumpeterian model with two sectors: consumption and investment, and two types of firms: state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately owned enterprises (POEs). Within this framework, multi-product firms require fixed inputs of investment goods to operate — a resource that is also crucial for firm expansion, and the soft budget constraint allows subsidized firms to continue operating on loss-making product lines. This distortion raises the price of investment goods, suppresses firm dynamics, and dampens aggregate growth. To quantify the mechanism, the model is calibrated using Chinese firm-level data. Our quantitative exercise shows that eliminating the SOE soft budget constraint friction reduces the price of investment goods by 9.82 percent, increases the overall TFP growth rate by 0.12 percentage points, and generates a welfare gain of 4.94 percent.

CTI identifies time—specifically lawful delay and institutional sequencing—as an implicit but enforceable constitutional variable already embedded within the architecture of Articles I–III. Bicameralism, staggered elections, deliberative procedure, presentment, and judicial finality operate collectively as temporal safeguards, ensuring that democratic pressure matures into binding authority only after surviving durability, contestation, and reconsideration.

The Article introduces a novel interpretive framework—the Constitutional Temporal Mirror Paradox—to explain a recurring modern misdiagnosis: institutions designed to operate across time are increasingly evaluated within cultural and informational environments optimized for immediacy. Under conditions of temporal compression, lawful delay is perceived as dysfunction, restraint as evasion, and sequence as failure. This perceptual inversion generates pressure for extra-constitutional substitution through executive acceleration, administrative improvisation, or indirect expressive control—not because the Constitution is deficient, but because its temporal logic is misunderstood.

CTI further identifies a generational dimension to this misdiagnosis. Earlier cohorts of citizens and lawmakers carried lived experience of delay as a formative constraint, internalizing patience, endurance, and proportionality through necessity rather than instruction. As generational turnover proceeds, that experiential memory diminishes by attrition. Newer cohorts—no less capable or legitimate—enter civic life under conditions of simultaneity, where expression, acknowledgment, and reaction are structurally compressed. In such environments, fulfillment is intuitively associated with immediacy, and delay appears anomalous rather than constitutive. This shift does not reflect diminished civic virtue, but a structural change in how democratic actors encounter time itself.

CTI advances constitutional law by restoring the proper object of evaluation. It reaffirms First Amendment absolutism by locating stabilization entirely downstream of expression and upstream of coercive authority. Speech remains free—even when destabilizing. Constitutional discipline applies only to when power may lawfully bind, not to what may be said, believed, or amplified. Accordingly, the doctrine operates outside content regulation, platform governance, and policy prescription, and proposes no new rights, standards of review, or reallocations of institutional power.

Jurisdictionally, CTI is modest. It does not supply courts with a new test or invite outcome-driven adjudication. Instead, it clarifies an existing constitutional distinction: courts may assess structural legality, procedural durability, and temporal sequence, while remaining barred from adjudicating the truth, harm, or desirability of speech or political outcomes. In this sense, CTI functions as an interpretive lens rather than an operational mandate—one that aligns with separation-of-powers doctrine, judicial restraint, and established First Amendment jurisprudence.

Ultimately, the Article argues that no constitutional amendment is required. The Constitution is not silent; it is misunderstood. Democratic legitimacy is not strengthened by speed, but by survivability. By recovering time as a constitutional safeguard, CTI preserves liberty without censorship, authority without haste, and democratic responsiveness without sacrificing endurance. The Republic survives not by accelerating power, but by insisting that power earn the right to endure.

title: Engineering Away Economic Crises: The [C1/C2/τ] Meta-Architecture for Endogenous Stability and Dynamic Flow Equilibrium V2.0 Lite

detail.title: Engineering Away Economic Crises: The [C1/C2/τ] Meta-Architecture for Endogenous Stability and Dynamic Flow Equilibrium V2.0 Lite

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research is a purely theoretical academic exploration. The authors have not received any direct financial benefit from it, nor are there any associated commercial entities or political projects. The C1/C2/τ meta-architecture described herein is an open economic engineering design blueprint.

detail.abstract: This paper diagnoses that the root cause of contemporary macroeconomic cyclical crises lies in two structural paradoxes within the economic system: the "functional conflict of money" and the "spatiotemporal dissonance in governance."To thoroughly cure this issue, we propose the Economic Engineering [C1/C2/τ] Meta-Architecture. Through monetary function decoupling (the C1/C2 dual-track digital currency system) and the embedding of the τ friction endogenous automatic stabilizer, this architecture synthesizes theories from multiple disciplines such as mechanism design, system dynamics, and cybernetics, thereby laying a new foundation for the economic system endowed with endogenous stability.We prove that macroeconomic stability will strictly adhere to Dynamic Flow Equilibrium (DFE), transforming from a probabilistic policy target into a system property guaranteed by mathematical certainty.This work signifies a fundamental shift in economic methodology: from a "science of choice" that seeks solutions under given constraints, to a "social engineering" that focuses on the optimal design of the constraints themselves.

title:
Faith, Tech, and the Mob 
A Formal Theory of Authoritarian Cost-Reduction

detail.title:
Faith, Tech, and the Mob 
A Formal Theory of Authoritarian Cost-Reduction
detail.abstract: Why do rational authoritarian regimes, equipped with precise digital surveillance tools, choose to empower volatile religious mobs? This paper challenges a critical assumption of digital authoritarianism (DA) literature, namely that regimes invest in technology to raise the material cost of dissent. I argue that regimes are adopting a new strategy-sacralized digital authoritarianism (SDA)-which fuses algorithmic capacity with sacred legitimacy to fundamentally alter the utility calculus of repression. I formalize this logic using a global game model with strategic complementarities, introducing two parameters: sacralization (λ) and digital crowdsourcing (δ). The equilibrium analysis demonstrates that by framing repression as a spiritual duty and providing digital platforms for coordination, regimes can lower the "minimum necessary grievance" (θ) required for incentivizing citizens to repress, bypassing the fiscal and political costs of traditional coercion. I test these predictions using comparative evidence from Turkey, Pakistan, China, India, and Myanmar. I find that SDA regimes successfully create a selfsustaining equilibrium of violence that is more cost-efficient than DA and solves the "problem of authoritarian control" without empowering the military. The findings suggest that the future of authoritarian resilience lies not in the precision of the police state, but in the algorithmic coordination of the faithful.

title: Effect of Off-Farm and on-Farm Capital Formation among Small Scale Rice Farmers in Benue State, Nigeria
affiliations: Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University

detail.title: Effect of Off-Farm and on-Farm Capital Formation among Small Scale Rice Farmers in Benue State, Nigeria
detail.abstract: The study investigated the effects of off-farm and on-farm capital formation among small-scale rice farmers in Benue State, Nigeria. 752 respondents were selected across six local governments using multi-stage sampling technique. Data for the study was collected by the use of well-structured questionnaire. Descriptive and inferential statistics were the statistical tools used for the analysis. Two hypotheses were formulated; multinomial logit and one way ANOVA models were used to test the relationship between off-farm and on-farm capital formation among small-scale rice farmers in the study area. The result on socioeconomic characteristics of rice farmers showed that majority (77.39%) were male with average of 39years, most (45.21%) has post-secondary school education with a household of 6persons. The average farming experience of 7years, 0.6hectares farm size, 68.20% had extension contact and land ownership was mostly rented (37.16%). The result on the nature of off-farm work engaged by small-scale rice farmers was mostly non-agricultural wage employment (42.15%). The results on capital position of small-scale rice farmers show that, agricultural wage employment has the highest current ratio (147,381.8), capital turn over ratio (4.101) and profit to asset ratio (0.7929). The capital position of current ratio is higher with a mean of 125.1136, followed by capital turnover ratio with a mean 3.738731. Profit to asset ratio has the lowest with a mean of 0.7636289. This implies that small-scale rice farmers in Benue State earn very low incomes from farming due to low output prices and the pressure to sell immediately after harvest to cater for immediate family needs. The coefficient of Mills Lambda was significant at 5% level, which showed that there is a significant difference in the choice of off-farm typologies in the study area. The result on off-farm income among small-scale rice farmers showed that agricultural wage employment (251,734), non-agricultural wage employment (35,814.61), employment (140,307.3). The result to capital position development of small scale rice farmers showed lack of access to public credit facilities (4.302), lack f access to mechanization (4.252), high interest rate of commercial banks loan (4.126) and high cost of fertilizers (4.045).The results also showed that most of the small-scale rice farmers do not own personal land with a corresponding capital position. The intensive constraints to capital position of the small-scale rice farmers constitute an impediment to effective business performance. The study concluded that involvement in off-farm work enhanced farm income and income diversification is an essential livelihood strategy among small-scale rice farmers in the study area. Finally, the study recommended that Benue State Government should render adequate support to small-scale rice farmers such as provision of adequate credit, agricultural input, intelligence and market news in order to buttress their efforts in the business.

title: Land Borrowed by the Sun: Ecological Trade-offs of China's Subsidized Photovoltaic Development
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Land Borrowed by the Sun: Ecological Trade-offs of China's Subsidized Photovoltaic Development
detail.abstract: Motivated by growing concerns over ecological sustainability and cleanliness of energy, solar photovoltaic (PV) projects have attracted significant attention in China and globally. Employing a difference-indifferences (DID) model and a comprehensive multi-dimensional dataset that includes information on ecological environment, government officials, photovoltaic enterprises, and participating farmers, this study examines the potential ecological challenges arising from the expansion of PV projects. Our results indicate that while photovoltaic projects promote regional economic development and increase household income, they generate only a slight positive environmental effect and also entail certain negative environmental impacts. We construct a "government-enterprise-household" analytical framework to capture the action of main actors involved in photovoltaic projects, identifying three key mechanisms driving these negative ecological consequences. Firstly, government-level incentives: The promotion tournament among local officials leads to an overemphasis on the economic benefits of PV projects at the expense of ecological considerations. Secondly, enterprise behavior: Profit-driven motives incentivize firms to enter the industry primarily for subsidies, potentially resulting in regulatory violations. Thirdly, household participation: Some farmers lease land to PV enterprises without adequate oversight, while others install PV panels themselves but lack environmental awareness, neglecting ecological preservation. Further analysis reveals that environmental regulations of the government, including adjustments in regulatory institutions and development models, effectively mitigate these adverse effects. Strengthening supervision over private enterprises and optimizing subsidy policies emerge as critical reform directions for future PV support measures.

title: Optimal Use of Preferences in Artificial Intelligence Algorithms
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Use of Preferences in Artificial Intelligence Algorithms
detail.abstract: Machine learning systems embed preferences either in training losses or through post-processing of calibrated predictions. Applying information design methods from Strack and Yang (2024), this paper provides decision-problem-agnostic conditions under which separation-training preference-free and applying preferences ex post is optimal. Unlike prior work that requires specifying downstream objectives, the welfare results here apply uniformly across decision problems. The key primitive is a diminishing-value-of-information condition: relative to a fixed (normalised) preferencefree loss, preference embedding makes informativeness less valuable at the margin, inducing a mean-preserving contraction of learned posteriors. Because the value of information is convex in beliefs, preference-free training weakly dominates for any expected-utility decision problem. This provides theoretical foundations for modular AI pipelines that learn calibrated probabilities and implement asymmetric costs through downstream decision rules. However, separation requires users to implement optimal decision rules. When cognitive constraints bind-as documented in human-AI decision-making-preference embedding can dominate by automating threshold computation. These results provide design guidance: preserve optionality through postprocessing when objectives may shift; embed preferences when decision-stage frictions dominate.

title: How Parenting Experiences Differ Between,Chinese Mothers and Fathers of Young Children
affiliations: , Henan University, University of Nebraska-Lincoln and

detail.title: How Parenting Experiences Differ Between,Chinese Mothers and Fathers of Young Children
detail.abstract: The current study explores parenting experiences of mothers and fathers and their perceived child behavior problems within a contemporary Chinese cultural context. Data were collected from 2,519 Chinese parents, including 2,034 mothers and 485 fathers with children aged 3 to 6 in Henan province. Analyses included independent samples t-tests and multi-group structural equation modeling by parental gender. Results revealed significant gender differences in maternal and paternal parenting experiences and perceived child behavioral outcomes. Compared to fathers, mothers reported less coparenting support from and for their partners, higher levels of parenting stress, less physical and emotional neglect, and fewer behavior problems in children. There were variations in latent constructs of coparenting relationships and child maltreatment, and significant differences in associations between parenting experiences and child behavior problems based on parental gender. Findings suggest including both mothers and fathers in parenting research and programs to ultimately benefit child behavioral outcomes.

title: Electoral Results affect beliefs about the Past: Evidence from Chile
affiliations: McGill University - Department of Economics, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and Institute for Advanced Study in Toulouse

detail.title: Electoral Results affect beliefs about the Past: Evidence from Chile
detail.abstract: Can electoral outcomes shape voters' perceptions of the past? We argue that electoral outcomes provide informational cues that prompt voters to reinterpret prior conditions, shifting the benchmarks on which accountability rests. We focus on perceptions of crime, a valence issue that voters likely take into account when choosing any candidate. We propose that perceptions of crime change immediately after an election, as voters reinterpret prior conditions through the lens of the relevance of crime in the winning candidate's platform. We leverage the timing of opinion surveys in Chile on public security to compare respondents interviewed just before and just after local elections, across municipalities where a right-wing mayor narrowly won versus narrowly lost. We show that shortly after a local right-wing candidate wins by a small margin, respondents report that their neighborhood, state, and country are less safe than those who answered the same survey a few days before the election. Victimization, which is unlikely to be misremembered, does not vary across groups of respondents. The findings show that this shift in perceptions directly affects electoral accountability: When political outcomes shape beliefs about past performance, accountability itself becomes endogenous to electoral results.

title: Digital Convenience in Credit Markets
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Banking & Finance and Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Banking & Finance

detail.title: Digital Convenience in Credit Markets
detail.abstract: We analyze how digital convenience affects competition in lending markets. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that a lender offering high convenience can lose to a traditional lender with low convenience, even if the former has better creditworthiness screening ability. A lender with high convenience may charge higher rates, but also attracts more borrowers with higher default rates, thereby worsening the overall risk profile of the lender's borrower pool. Our findings not only explain the recent decline of peer-to-peer lending and the lax screening of some Buy Now, Pay Later lenders, but also shed light on the slow digitalization in the insurance and over-the-counter trading markets.

title: Epistemic Decision Statistics: A Manifesto for Credibility-aware Statistical Governance

detail.title: Epistemic Decision Statistics: A Manifesto for Credibility-aware Statistical Governance
detail.abstract: Modern statistics excels at parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, and uncertainty quantification. However, it provides limited formal guidance on how probabilistic outputs should be translated into operational decisions under epistemic risk. In practice, scalar indicators such as p-values, confidence intervals, posterior probabilities, and performance metrics are frequently treated as direct proxies for trustworthiness, despite their sensitivity to model assumptions, sampling variability, and distributional fragility. This gap has become increasingly consequential in highstakes domains such as clinical decision-making, automated systems, and regulatory governance, where numerical confidence may conceal epistemic instability and decision risk. This paper introduces Epistemic Decision Statistics (EDS) as a foundational discipline concerned with governing the admissibility, credibility, and stability of statistical decisions under uncertainty. EDS does not replace statistical inference; rather, it formalizes the epistemic layer that regulates when, how, and whether inferential outputs may be operationally acted upon. The framework rests on five pillars: (i) epistemic geometry, in which uncertainty is structured into credibility zones rather than scalar thresholds; (ii) prioritization of decision credibility over statistical significance; (iii) a governance layer implementing action admissibility rules, confidence suppression, abstention protocols, and recalibration triggers; (iv) explicit modeling of epistemic stability, fragility, and inflation dynamics; and (v) cross-paradigm unification spanning frequentist, Bayesian, likelihood-based, and machine-learning inference. We formalize the core axioms of EDS, propose a layered epistemic governance architecture, and demonstrate conceptual continuity through existing instantiations in zonal inference, Bayesian epistemic zoning, and epistemic likelihood testing. EDS reframes statistics not only as a science of estimation, but as a discipline of credibility-aware decision governance.

title: Economic Development and the Environment
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and Yale University

detail.title: Economic Development and the Environment
detail.abstract:
Economic development relies on and transforms the environment. The transformation is evident in the poor environmental quality in many developing countries. For example, air quality in Southeast Asia is three times worse than in the United States, in sub-Saharan Africa four times worse and in South Asia more than six times worse. We model how environmental quality affects health, productivity and well-being and how individuals privately adapt to environmental hazards. We also model how collective action and formal regulation contribute to environmental quality. We draw three main findings from a review of empirical research on these mechanisms. First, individual adaptation to environmental hazards is both inadequate as a remedy and inefficiently low. Second, collective action, without the state, to manage resources or address externalities has been outstripped by the scale of environmental problems. Third, state action through formal regulation works better than it looks. Many formal regulations are coarse, poorly targeted and inefficient, but nonetheless yield benefits in excess of their costs.

title: The Polarization Threshold: Consensus Breakdown in Belief Dynamics with Cognitive Dissonance

detail.title: The Polarization Threshold: Consensus Breakdown in Belief Dynamics with Cognitive Dissonance

declarations.funderStatement: DS4H interdisciplinary scholarship

detail.abstract: When does a society that shares common information converge toward consensus, and when does it fracture into persistent ideological camps? This chapter establishes conditions under which a polarisation threshold κ ⋆ > 0 exists: when cognitively realistic agents-who anchor to prior beliefs, face costly belief revision, and observe a social consensus signalinteract under mean-field coupling, consensus is stable if and only if social exposure κ lies below κ ⋆. Under spectral regularity of the linearised Fokker-Planck operator, the threshold is uniquely determined by the balance between individual restoring forces (anchoring, cognitive resets) and social amplification, without requiring heterogeneous priors, bounded confidence, or network structure. We characterise κ ⋆ via spectral analysis, establish a center-manifold reduction yielding a pitchfork normal form, and characterise the local bifurcation structure via center-manifold reduction, yielding a pitchfork normal form whose cubic coefficient b determines whether polarization emerges smoothly (supercritical, b > 0) or discontinuously (subcritical, b < 0).

title: College Major Choice, Payoffs, and Gender Gaps
affiliations: University of Chicago Booth School of Business, University of Chile, Independent and University of Chile

detail.title: College Major Choice, Payoffs, and Gender Gaps
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how college major choices shape earnings and fertility outcomes. Using administrative data that link students' preferences, random assignment to majors, and post-college outcomes, we estimate the causal pecuniary and non-pecuniary returns to different fields of study. We document substantial heterogeneity in these returns across majors and show that such variation helps explain gender gaps in labor market outcomes: women place greater weight on balancing career and family in their major choices, and these preference differences account for about 30% of the gender earnings gap among college graduates. Last, we use our causal estimates to evaluate the effects of counterfactual assignment rules that target representation gaps in settings with centralized assignment systems. We find that gender quotas in high-return fields can significantly reduce representation and earnings gaps with minimal impacts on efficiency and aggregate fertility.

title: Simple and Advanced Reflexivity in GDPR Enforcement: Empirical Evidence from DPA Activity
affiliations: University of Wroclaw - Faculty of Law, Administration and Economics and University of Wrocław

detail.title: Simple and Advanced Reflexivity in GDPR Enforcement: Empirical Evidence from DPA Activity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal or institutional relationships resulting in conflicts of interest, or other influence, related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Does not apply
declarations.funderStatement: The article is based on research funded by the Polish National Science Centre (research project 2016/23/B/HS5/00873: ‘Models of Legal Regulation of Risk in the Light of the Theory of Reflexivity’).

detail.abstract:
- The GDPR has introduced a reflexive approach to data protection in the European Union, based among others on meta-regulation, risk-based approach, double-loop learning, and regulatory pyramids.
- There is no empirical evidence of whether the EU member states have effectively implemented the strategy of reflexive regulation in data protection. The paper offers a case study of the DPA in Poland to answer this question.
- The researched DPA has successfully adopted simple reflexivity that allows for ad-hoc, case-to-case reflexive enforcement. Still, the absence of more advanced and principled forms of reflexive data protection may jeopardise the objectives of GDPR.
- One of the main reasons for incomplete reflexivity on the part of DPAs is that the GDPR contains inconsistencies and promotes reflexivity of data controllers but not of supervisory authorities.

title: The Informational Role of Emission Markets: Prices vs Quantities with Dispersed Information About Externalities
affiliations: University of Arizona - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Informational Role of Emission Markets: Prices vs Quantities with Dispersed Information About Externalities
detail.abstract:
I study asymmetric information about the social cost of an externality, as opposed to asymmetric information about private costs of abatement. I show that quantity regulation with bankable permits has an informational advantage because the permit market aggregates dispersed information about social costs. It has the disadvantage of making private costs more uncertain ex ante. I analytically derive the expression for the (dis)advantage of prices over quantities in this setting. I show that a quantity policy can dominate a price policy for any slope of marginal private costs and always dominates when marginal private costs are sufficiently flat.

title: Betrayal Aversion in Human-AI Interaction
affiliations: and University of Göttingen

detail.title: Betrayal Aversion in Human-AI Interaction
detail.abstract: We examine whether AI agents, specifically large language models (LLMs), attenuate betrayal aversion. In a pre-registered experiment, we analyze trust games where agents decide for trustees with no monetary consequences for themselves. This pure agency setting isolates betrayal from self interest and mirrors how LLMs typically operate. We measure betrayal aversion as the difference in minimal acceptable probabilities of reciprocation between trust games and risky lotteries. Comparing human versus AI agents, we find that betrayal aversion persists in pure agency settings but is significantly reduced with AI: from 4.22 to 1.61 percentage points in the full sample and from 8.5 to 5.3 percentage points among betrayal-averse participants. Control conditions confirm this holds when accounting for intrinsic preferences toward human or AI interaction. Our findings suggest that deploying AI agents in trust-sensitive contexts such as lending, hiring, and customer service may reduce the psychological barriers to cooperate.

title: Compatibility Theorems for Generalized N-Person Games

detail.title: Compatibility Theorems for Generalized N-Person Games
detail.abstract: This article introduces the notion of compatibility to facilitate the study of the symmetries that exist between desiderata models within the class of abstract economy. Specifically, the article elucidates sufficient and necessary conditions to declare conventional models equivalent. The resulting theory --- compatibility theory --- provides the framework for the systematic study of these invariants.

title: Does Generative AI Crowd Out Human Creators? Evidence from Pixiv
affiliations: Korea Development Institute (KDI), Department of Economics and New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Does Generative AI Crowd Out Human Creators? Evidence from Pixiv
detail.abstract:
Using a comprehensive dataset of posts from a major platform for anime- and manga-style artwork, we study the impact of the launch of a prominent text-to-image generative AI. Focusing on the majority of incumbent creators who do not adopt AI as a primary tool, we show that the AI launch led to a significant decline in post uploads by illustrators, whereas comic artists were less affected, reflecting the need for tight stylistic alignment across sequential images in comics. We present empirical evidence for two underlying mechanisms. First, illustration posts experience a loss of viewer attention, measured by bookmarks, following the AI launch, which can significantly harm creators’ business models. Second, direct competition from AI-generated content plays an important role: illustrators working on intellectual properties (IPs, such as Pokémon) that are more heavily invaded by AI reduce their uploads disproportionately more. We further examine creators’ responses and show that illustrators with greater exposure to AI avoid using tags favored by AI-generated content after the AI launch and broaden the range of IPs they work on, consistent with a risk-hedging response to AI invasion.

title: The Twenty-four Hour Economy or Rolled-up Sidewalks: Trends in Work Timing and Their Causes
affiliations: University of Notre Dame and Columbia University - Barnard College

detail.title: The Twenty-four Hour Economy or Rolled-up Sidewalks: Trends in Work Timing and Their Causes
detail.abstract:
We demonstrate nearly steady trends from 1973-2023 in the U.S. in the timing of when people work for pay, away from evening and night hours toward “usual” daytime hours. The trend is related to changes in rising educational attainment, to increased real incomes, and the increased wage premium for undesirable work times—evenings and nights—that we document. The trend exists in all major industries except retail, in which changes in technology biased work away from daytime hours. The trend was accelerated by the sharp increase in telework that occurred after the Covid pandemic, an increase that was especially concentrated during daytime hours. While we observe the same phenomenon in France from 1966 to 2010, we do not in the U.K. from 1974-2015, arguably because of the very sharp decline in unionization in the U.K. and the changes in retailing.

title: Main Criteria For The Classification Of Disinfor-Mation And Attempts To Criminalisation Of Its Spread In Ukraine

detail.title: Main Criteria For The Classification Of Disinfor-Mation And Attempts To Criminalisation Of Its Spread In Ukraine

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published in the Bratislava Law Review (https://blr.flaw.uniba.sk/index.php/BLR/about).

detail.abstract: Based on the methodology of documentary review of scientific sources, available materials of public organisations, the judicial practices in investigating cases of disinformation spread, Ukrainian and foreign sources, the process of disinformation propagation has been researched. Using this approach, the main criteria for classifying disinformation by domains, objectives, methods, sources, forms, and channels were formulated. It was found that in Ukraine, there is still no unified legislative practice to counter disinformation, which leads to the uncontrolled application of manipulative processes and the dissemination of unreliable information by hostile intelligence services. Mass media and other channels of disinformation dissemination continue to evade the attention of law enforcement agencies, for instance, in the fields of economics, science, education, culture, and sports.

title: Government Bonds Supply Shocks

detail.title: Government Bonds Supply Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of government bond supply news shocks on debt prices. I exploit an institutional feature in the UK fiscal policy framework and high frequency identification to estimate the effect of a large government bond increase, which is not due to news about the fiscal deficit and total debt. The identification is based upon the price changes of futures on gilts around news published by the UK Debt Management Office in general and especially just after the budget speeches of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. While these speeches discuss fiscal policy and overall debt forecasts, they do not disclose the exact supply of government bonds. I find that a 1 percentage point increase in government bonds increases interest rates on a 10-year government bond by 9 basis points and the corporate bond risk spread by 2 basis points. My results are consistent with the preferred habitat theory of interest rates where constrained arbitrageurs arbitrage across both government and corporate debt markets. The paper suggests that fiscal policy transmits also through direct crowding-out in debt markets.

title: Unpacking The Savings Puzzle In The Western Balkans: Remittances, Financial Depth, And Macroeconomic Stability
affiliations: and University of New York Tirana

detail.title: Unpacking The Savings Puzzle In The Western Balkans: Remittances, Financial Depth, And Macroeconomic Stability
detail.abstract: The determinants of gross national savings in the Western Balkans present a complex puzzle, characterized by transitioning economies, significant remittance inflows, and evolving financial systems. This study seeks to unravel this puzzle by empirically investigating the roles of macroeconomic stability, financial depth, and remittances across Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia (2007–2023). Employing a panel data approach, a random effects model was selected to analyze these relationships. The model was rigorously validated through diagnostic tests for multicollinearity, autocorrelation, and cross-sectional dependence. Our findings reveal a nuanced picture: while GDP per capita growth, remittances, and money supply act as significant pieces of the savings puzzle by positively bolstering savings, other factors create tension. Unemployment, inflation, and domestic credit to the private sector significantly negatively impact savings, revealing critical tradeoffs. The COVID-19 pandemic shock further underscored the region's economic vulnerability by disrupting savings patterns. We conclude that solving the savings puzzle requires holistic policies that promote macroeconomic stability to mitigate vulnerabilities, harness financial depth without discouraging savings, and strategically leverage remittance inflows for enhanced financial resilience.

title: Current Account Deficits and the Welfare of Future Generations
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis

detail.title: Current Account Deficits and the Welfare of Future Generations
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the effects of one nation's taxation of consumption on the welfare of future generations of other countries. To do this, it presents an otherwise standard one-good, two-country optimal growth model with free capital markets, but where each date represents the lifetime of a generation which cares not only about its own consumption and leisure, but also that of its descendants.Relative to a no tax benchmark, a policy of one country taxing consumption of its initial generations has ambiguous welfare effects for future generations of the other country, as long as those future generations are not too far in the future. Higher initial savings in the first country raises capital levels, and thus wages, in both countries, raising welfare of future generations in the second country, but also induces lower bequests in the second country, lowering the welfare of its future generations. In the long run, or for generations born near the steady state, the welfare effects of the first country inducing lower consumption of its initial generations are unambiguous: future generations of the second country are made worse off. Households born in the second country will regret that their ancestors allowed such policy-induced intertemporal trade.

title: War and Democratic Backsliding
affiliations: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management and Einaudi Institute for Economics and Finance (EIEF)

detail.title: War and Democratic Backsliding
detail.abstract:
We provide the first global, long-run evidence on how war reshapes democratic institutions. Using data on all conflicts since 1948, we show that the onset of conflict causes a large and persistent decline in democracy: institutions weaken immediately, continue to erode for nearly a decade, and do not recover. Yet this deterioration is highly selective. It appears only in first-time conflicts, intrastate wars, highly fractionalized societies, and conflicts that governments win. The decline operates through political channels – media censorship, judicial purges, curtailed civil liberties, irregular leadership turnover, and constitutional suspensions - rather than through any functional requirement of war-making. Autocratization does not increase the probability of victory, and institutional instability reduces it. Taken together, the findings show that war does not require autocracy; it enables executives to expand their authority and implement institutional changes that would be difficult to enact in peacetime.

title: The United States as an Active Industrial Policy Nation
affiliations: Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance, PBCSF, Tsinghua University and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance

detail.title: The United States as an Active Industrial Policy Nation
detail.abstract:
We document and characterize a new history of U.S. federal-level industrial policies by scanning all 12,167 Congressional Acts and 6,030 Presidential Orders from 1973 through 2022. We find several interesting patterns. First, contrary to a common perception, the United States has always been an active industrial policy nation throughout the period, regardless of which party is in power, with 5.4 laws and 3.4 Presidential Orders per year on average containing new industrial policies. Second, we identify roughly 300% more instances of industrial policies than those in the Global Trade Alert (GTA) database during 2008-2022, despite using essentially the same definition. Third, industrial policies in practice are as likely to be justified by national security as by economic competitiveness. Fourth, many U.S. industrial policies incorporate design features that help mitigate potential drawbacks, such as explicit expiration dates and pilot programs for emerging technologies. Finally, based on stock market reactions and firm performance, the identified policies are recognized as economically significant in shifting resource allocations.

title: The Demand for Grandchildren: Children as Family Public Goods and Implications for Cooperative Bargaining
affiliations: University of Manitoba - Department of Economics and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: The Demand for Grandchildren: Children as Family Public Goods and Implications for Cooperative Bargaining
detail.abstract:
The title says it all. Well, almost all. To economists, the situation suggests bargaining between parents and grandparents, where the grandparents can "bribe" the parents to have more children or to have children sooner than they otherwise would. Because cash transfers seem inappropriate, bribes are likely to take the form of promises of child care or down payments on houses. Coasian bargaining or, more generally, cooperative bargaining models with their explicit assumption of Pareto efficiency offer accessible off-the shelf models. Larger family size (e.g., the participation of both pairs of grandparents) and family complexity (e.g., resulting from divorce and repartnering in the parents' generation or the grandparents' generation) threaten the assumption of zero or low transaction costs. Low transaction costs, explicit in the Coasian analysis and implicit in cooperative game theory's assumption of Pareto efficiency, play a crucial role. The generalization of family economics from the analysis of bargaining between spouses to include family members beyond the household will at some point require replacing Coasian and cooperative bargaining with models of noncooperative bargaining.

title: A Few Bad Apples? Academic Dishonesty, Political Selection, and Institutional Performance in China
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and University of Chicago

detail.title: A Few Bad Apples? Academic Dishonesty, Political Selection, and Institutional Performance in China
detail.abstract:
Honesty is perceived as fundamental to societal functioning, motivating education systems worldwide to enforce strict oversight and heavy penalties for dishonest behavior. Yet much academic misconduct remains unexposed, and its broader consequences are further obscured by the sorting of individuals into careers based on probity. Applying advanced plagiarism-detection algorithms to half a million publicly available graduate dissertations in China, we uncover hidden misconduct and validate it against incentivized measures of honesty. Linking plagiarism records to rich administrative data, we document four main findings. First, plagiarism is pervasive and predicts adverse political selection: plagiarists are more likely to enter and advance in the public sector. Second, plagiarists perform worse when holding power: focusing on the judiciary and exploiting quasi-random case assignments, we find that judges with plagiarism histories issue more preferential rulings and attract a greater number of appeals — effects partly mitigated by trial livestreaming. Third, plagiarizing judges generate spillovers onto other judges and lawyers. Fourth, exploiting the staggered adoption of detection tools, we demonstrate that enforcing academic integrity leads to modest improvements in future professional conduct.

We leverage Becker’s time allocation theory to examine consumer demand and market competition for time-intensive goods. The Beckerian model predicts higher diversion ratios for goods with substantial time shares and those with high time costs relative to monetary prices. Applying this model to data from two field experiments, we analyze demand for Facebook and Instagram, focusing on substitution patterns across online activities and offline time use. Our findings indicate that users exhibit low elasticity to ad load, the primary user cost, and that time shares and time costs significantly influence diversion ratios. We explore the implications for user costs and benefits on these platforms and assess the potential impact of a Federal Trade Commission-proposed de-merger of Facebook and Instagram.

title: Modernizing the IRS in the Age of AI
affiliations: Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law

detail.title: Modernizing the IRS in the Age of AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 718

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful tools for modernizing tax administration, from automating audits and improving fraud detection to enhancing taxpayer services. But if deployed prematurely, AI risks entrenching the very flaws it aims to fix. The Internal Revenue Service remains burdened by outdated infrastructure, fragmented data systems, limited transparency, and enforcement disparities. Without foundational reform, AI will not increase efficiency or equity. Instead, it will amplify structural shortcomings and obscure accountability. This article argues that the Internal Revenue Service cannot responsibly adopt AI without first addressing its systemic weaknesses in governance, data infrastructure, and legal oversight. Drawing on lessons from prior modernization failures, this article demonstrates that piecemeal upgrades and underfunded initiatives have repeatedly stalled progress. It further contends that recent efforts to defund the Internal Revenue Service threaten to sabotage the very reforms necessary to support responsible, effective automation. 

Thus, rather than viewing AI as a shortcut to reform, this article makes the case for a deliberate, sequenced approach: modernization first, AI second. Through institutional restructuring, sustained investment, and the development of transparent and accountable data practices, the Internal Revenue Service can build the foundation needed for AI to serve, not subvert, fair, effective, and efficient tax administration. Ultimately, the future of AI in tax administration depends not on how fast it is adopted, but on how responsibly it is implemented.

title: Behavioral Economics of AI: LLM Biases and Corrections

detail.title: Behavioral Economics of AI: LLM Biases and Corrections
detail.abstract:
Do generative AI models, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit systematic behavioral biases in economic and financial decisions? If so, how can these biases be mitigated? Drawing on the cognitive psychology and experimental economics literatures, we conduct the most comprehensive set of experiments to date—originally designed to document human biases—on prominent LLM families across model versions and scales. We document systematic patterns in LLM behavior. In preference-based tasks, responses become more human-like as models become more advanced or larger, while in belief-based tasks, advanced large-scale models frequently generate rational responses. Prompting LLMs to make rational decisions reduces biases.

detail.title: Scaling Sustainable Investing in Emerging and Developing Economies: Frictions and Opportunities
detail.abstract:
Mobilizing private capital at scale is critical for financing sustainable development, particularly in emerging and developing economies (EMDEs), where capital is most needed. We conduct a global survey of senior investment decision-makers across a broad spectrum of capital providers, including asset managers, pension and sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, philanthropic investors, and others. The survey provides novel evidence on investors’ risk-return expectations, risk perceptions, and investment practices in EMDEs and in blended finance structures. We document four main findings. First, conditional on investor type, return expectations in EMDEs are comparable to those in developed markets, suggesting that categorical exclusions of EMDE assets might be inefficient. Second, investors’ dominant risk perceptions—particularly currency and political risks—are poorly aligned with the de-risking tools commonly employed in blended finance. Third, prevailing approaches to evaluating blended finance rely on both input- and outcome-based metrics, yet with limited measurement of financial and impact additionality. Fourth, our results highlight organizational and informational frictions, rather than unattractive financial fundamentals, as key barriers to scaling sustainable investing in EMDEs.
